stem: A 72-year-old woman tripped at home and landed on her outstretched left arm. An X-ray in the emergency department shows a fracture through the surgical neck of the humerus. Pinprick sensation is reduced over a small patch on the outer aspect of the upper arm just below the point of the shoulder. Sensation in the forearm and hand is normal, and she can extend her wrist and fingers. Which nerve has most likely been injured?
why_correct: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, so it is vulnerable in fractures here and in anterior shoulder dislocation. It supplies deltoid and teres minor and gives sensation to the regimental badge area over the lateral upper arm. Reduced sensation in exactly this patch after a surgical neck fracture points to axillary nerve injury.
why_wrong: A. Radial nerve injury follows mid-shaft fractures and causes wrist drop, but her wrist extension is intact. B. The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus and has no cutaneous area on the lateral arm. C. Long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula without arm numbness. D. Musculocutaneous nerve injury weakens elbow flexion and numbs the lateral forearm, not the shoulder.
pearl: Always test and document regimental badge sensation in surgical neck fractures and shoulder dislocations, both before and after any manipulation.
thinking: Fall onto outstretched arm ↓ Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus ↓ Nerve that wraps around the surgical neck ↓ Numb patch over lateral upper arm: regimental badge area ↓ Axillary nerve
exam_trap: A, radial nerve — the best-known nerve injury with humeral fractures, but it follows mid-shaft fractures and causes wrist drop; her wrist extension is normal.
takeaway: Surgical neck fracture with a numb regimental badge area: axillary nerve injury.

stem: A 19-year-old man who plays university football sees his GP about several episodes of a racing heartbeat over the past year. Each episode starts and stops abruptly and lasts a few minutes. Once it stopped when he strained hard while holding his breath. He has never fainted. Examination is normal. His resting ECG shows a shortened PR interval, with the initial part of each QRS complex slurred so that the QRS looks slightly broad. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A short PR interval with a slurred QRS upstroke (a delta wave) shows ventricular pre-excitation through an accessory pathway, and with paroxysmal palpitations this is Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. The pathway allows re-entrant tachycardias, which explains the abrupt episodes ended by a vagal manoeuvre. He needs cardiology referral, as catheter ablation of the pathway is usually curative.
why_wrong: A. Brugada syndrome shows coved ST elevation in the right chest leads, not a short PR with a delta wave. B. Long QT syndrome prolongs the QT interval and does not shorten the PR. C. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes left ventricular hypertrophy patterns and a murmur, not pre-excitation. E. First-degree heart block lengthens the PR interval rather than shortening it.
pearl: Pre-excitation triad on a resting ECG: short PR, delta wave and a slightly broad QRS. Palpitations plus this pattern means referral for electrophysiology assessment.
thinking: Young man with abrupt-onset palpitations ↓ Terminated by a vagal manoeuvre: re-entry ↓ Resting ECG: short PR with slurred QRS upstroke ↓ Delta wave means an accessory pathway ↓ Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome
exam_trap: C, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — a young athlete with palpitations makes HCM tempting, but the ECG describes pre-excitation, not hypertrophy, and examination is normal.
takeaway: Short PR plus delta wave with palpitations is Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome.

stem: A 46-year-old man books a GP appointment because a pharmacy blood pressure check gave a high reading. In the surgery his blood pressure is 156/98 mmHg, and a second reading a few minutes later is 152/96 mmHg. He feels well. His fundi are normal and his urine dipstick is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.C: Offer ambulatory blood pressure monitoring to confirm the diagnosis
options.D: Recheck his blood pressure in five years
options.E: Repeat clinic readings at three further appointments, then diagnose

correct_answer: C. Offer ambulatory blood pressure monitoring to confirm the diagnosis
why_correct: NICE recommends confirming a raised clinic blood pressure with ambulatory blood pressure monitoring, or home monitoring if ABPM is unsuitable, before diagnosing hypertension, to exclude a white-coat effect. Meanwhile, bloods, a urine albumin to creatinine ratio, an ECG and a cardiovascular risk assessment look for target-organ damage. Immediate treatment is reserved for severe readings or signs of target-organ damage, which he does not have.
why_wrong: A. Starting treatment before confirming the diagnosis risks treating white-coat hypertension. B. An ACE inhibitor may well be his eventual treatment, but drug choice comes only after the diagnosis is confirmed. D. A raised reading needs prompt confirmation, not a five-year wait. E. Further clinic readings cannot exclude a white-coat effect; out-of-clinic monitoring is needed.
pearl: If the clinic reading is high, take a second; if it differs substantially, take a third and record the lower. Then confirm with ABPM or home monitoring.
thinking: Raised clinic readings ↓ No symptoms, no signs of target-organ damage ↓ White-coat effect must be excluded ↓ Out-of-clinic monitoring is needed ↓ Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring
exam_trap: E, repeat clinic readings at three further appointments — repeated readings feel thorough, but they remain clinic readings and cannot exclude a white-coat effect.
takeaway: Confirm a raised clinic blood pressure with ABPM (or home monitoring) before diagnosing hypertension.

stem: A 72-year-old man tells his GP that for several weeks he has felt dizzy and very tired whenever he exerts himself. His pulse is regular at 38/min. Examining his neck, the GP sees intermittent large waves in the JVP, and the loudness of the first heart sound varies from beat to beat. A hospital ECG confirms that atrial and ventricular activity are completely dissociated. He takes amlodipine for hypertension, and his blood tests are normal. What is the definitive management?

options.B: IV atropine, then discharge once his heart rate improves
options.D: Stop amlodipine and review in six weeks

why_correct: Bradycardia with intermittent cannon waves, a variable first heart sound and AV dissociation on the ECG is complete heart block. As it is causing symptoms and there is no reversible cause, a permanent pacemaker is the definitive treatment. Atropine or temporary pacing may be used for stabilisation only.
why_wrong: B. Atropine is a short-term measure and does not treat the underlying block. C. An ICD treats ventricular tachyarrhythmias; the problem here is a conduction block needing pacing. D. Amlodipine does not slow AV conduction, so stopping it will not correct the block. E. The diagnosis is already confirmed, and delaying treatment of symptomatic complete heart block is unsafe.
pearl: Bedside clues to complete heart block: slow regular pulse, intermittent cannon waves in the JVP and a first heart sound that varies in loudness.
thinking: Exertional dizziness and fatigue ↓ Slow pulse with cannon waves and variable S1 ↓ AV dissociation confirmed: complete heart block ↓ Symptomatic, no reversible cause ↓ Permanent pacemaker
exam_trap: D, stop amlodipine and review — drug-induced block is a real cause, but amlodipine is a dihydropyridine that does not slow AV conduction, unlike verapamil or diltiazem.
takeaway: Symptomatic complete heart block is treated with a permanent pacemaker; atropine only buys time.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ602). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 72-year-old woman with ischaemic cardiomyopathy following an anterior myocardial infarction five years ago comes to the emergency department with an hour of palpitations. She is alert, her blood pressure is 112/70 mmHg and she has no chest pain or breathlessness. The ECG shows a regular broad-complex tachycardia at about 160/min. No previous ECG showing a bundle branch block is available. Until proven otherwise, which rhythm should this be treated as?

options.C: Sinus tachycardia with bundle branch block
options.D: Atrial flutter with 2:1 block and aberrant conduction

why_correct: A regular broad-complex tachycardia should be treated as ventricular tachycardia unless there is clear evidence otherwise, and previous myocardial infarction with structural heart disease makes VT by far the most likely cause. Treating VT as SVT, for example with verapamil, can cause collapse. Management follows the Resuscitation Council UK tachycardia algorithm with early expert help.
why_wrong: A. SVT with aberrancy is possible, but it should not be assumed, particularly after a myocardial infarction. C. Sinus tachycardia at this rate in a resting patient without a cause, and with no known bundle branch block, is unlikely. D. Atrial flutter with aberrancy is a diagnosis to be made only with clear evidence, not assumed. E. Pre-excited atrial fibrillation is irregular, whereas this rhythm is regular.
pearl: Broad-complex tachycardia after myocardial infarction is VT until proven otherwise. A normal blood pressure does not exclude VT.
thinking: Regular broad-complex tachycardia ↓ Previous infarction and cardiomyopathy ↓ No known pre-existing bundle branch block ↓ Assuming SVT risks giving harmful drugs ↓ Treat as ventricular tachycardia
exam_trap: A, supraventricular tachycardia with aberrant conduction — her stable blood pressure tempts you to think SVT, but haemodynamic stability does not exclude VT, and prior infarction makes VT the safe and likely assumption.
takeaway: A regular broad-complex tachycardia, especially after MI, is treated as VT until proven otherwise.

stem: A 66-year-old man sees his GP with three months of tiredness. He has no abdominal pain, change in bowel habit, rectal bleeding or indigestion, and does not take anti-inflammatory drugs. He eats a varied diet including meat. Blood tests show a low haemoglobin with a low MCV and a low ferritin. Coeliac serology is negative. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Oral iron, investigating only if the haemoglobin fails to improve
options.B: Urgent referral for upper and lower gastrointestinal investigation, starting oral iron
options.D: Repeat the full blood count in three months
options.E: Check vitamin B12 and folate levels

correct_answer: B. Urgent referral for upper and lower gastrointestinal investigation, starting oral iron
why_correct: Iron deficiency anaemia in a man, or a postmenopausal woman, without an obvious cause is presumed to be due to gastrointestinal blood loss until proven otherwise, and colorectal or gastric cancer must be excluded. He should be referred urgently for investigation of both the upper and lower gastrointestinal tract, and oral iron is started at the same time to replenish stores.
why_wrong: A. Treating with iron and waiting for a response delays the diagnosis of a possible cancer. C. Upper endoscopy alone may miss a colonic source; both ends need examining because lesions can coexist. D. Repeating the count only delays investigation of unexplained iron deficiency. E. B12 and folate deficiency cause macrocytosis, and the cause here is already established as iron deficiency.
pearl: Unexplained iron deficiency anaemia in a man or postmenopausal woman: test for coeliac disease and investigate both upper and lower GI tracts, while replacing iron.
thinking: Older man with microcytic anaemia ↓ Low ferritin confirms iron deficiency ↓ Diet adequate, no NSAIDs, coeliac negative ↓ Occult GI blood loss, possibly malignant ↓ Upper and lower GI investigation with oral iron
exam_trap: A, Oral iron, investigating only if the haemoglobin fails to improve — it treats the anaemia, but anaemia from a bleeding cancer can also respond to iron, so the cause must be found regardless.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency in an older man needs urgent upper and lower GI investigation, not just iron.

stem: A 64-year-old man tells his GP that for two months food has been sticking behind his breastbone. It started with bread and meat, and in the last few weeks even soup has been hard to get down. His trousers have become loose. He has smoked for 40 years and has had heartburn on and off for many years. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Trial of a proton pump inhibitor and review in 8 weeks
options.C: Urgent direct-access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy on a suspected cancer pathway

correct_answer: C. Urgent direct-access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy on a suspected cancer pathway
why_correct: Progressive dysphagia, first for solids and then liquids, with weight loss in an older smoker with long-standing reflux is an alarm presentation for oesophageal cancer. Dysphagia alone warrants an urgent direct-access upper gastrointestinal endoscopy on a suspected cancer pathway, which allows direct inspection and biopsy. Weight loss and his risk factors only add to the urgency.
why_wrong: A. An empirical acid suppression trial delays diagnosis and can mask symptoms. B. A barium swallow cannot provide tissue and is not the first-line urgent test. D. Routine referral is too slow for a suspected cancer. E. H. pylori testing is for uncomplicated dyspepsia, not dysphagia.
pearl: Dysphagia is always a red flag, regardless of age. Progression from solids to liquids suggests a mechanical, often malignant, obstruction.
thinking: Food sticking behind the sternum ↓ Progressing from solids to liquids ↓ Weight loss, smoking and long-standing reflux ↓ Suspected oesophageal cancer ↓ Urgent direct-access endoscopy
exam_trap: A, proton pump inhibitor trial — his long history of heartburn suggests reflux and a peptic stricture, but dysphagia with weight loss is an alarm feature that must not be treated empirically.
takeaway: Progressive dysphagia with weight loss needs urgent endoscopy on a suspected cancer pathway, not a PPI trial.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAAKT039). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 27-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes sees her GP because she feels exhausted all the time. She has iron deficiency anaemia despite light periods and a normal diet, and she has noticed intermittent loose, pale stools that are hard to flush, recurrent mouth ulcers, and an intensely itchy rash of small blisters on her elbows and knees. Her blood glucose control has recently become erratic, with several unexplained hypoglycaemic episodes. Which condition is most likely?
why_correct: Unexplained iron deficiency, steatorrhoea, mouth ulcers, an itchy blistering rash on extensor surfaces typical of dermatitis herpetiformis and erratic glucose control from malabsorption, in a woman with type 1 diabetes, point to coeliac disease. Autoimmune conditions such as type 1 diabetes increase its risk. Serology with tissue transglutaminase IgA and total IgA should be checked while she is still eating gluten.
why_wrong: A. Irritable bowel syndrome does not cause iron deficiency, steatorrhoea or a blistering rash. B. Crohn's disease can cause malabsorption and ulcers, but not dermatitis herpetiformis. C. Lactose intolerance causes bloating and diarrhoea after dairy, without malabsorption of iron or a rash. E. Pernicious anaemia causes B12 deficiency, not iron deficiency, steatorrhoea or a blistering rash.
pearl: Dermatitis herpetiformis is essentially pathognomonic of coeliac disease. Test anyone with unexplained iron deficiency or type 1 diabetes with new gastrointestinal symptoms.
thinking: Iron deficiency without blood loss ↓ Steatorrhoea, mouth ulcers and erratic glucose from malabsorption ↓ Itchy blistering rash on extensor surfaces ↓ Background type 1 diabetes ↓ Coeliac disease
exam_trap: B, Crohn's disease — mouth ulcers, diarrhoea and iron deficiency fit inflammatory bowel disease, but the itchy blistering extensor rash is dermatitis herpetiformis, which points to coeliac disease.
takeaway: Unexplained iron deficiency, malabsorption and dermatitis herpetiformis suggest coeliac disease; test on a gluten diet.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15725). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 71-year-old right-handed woman is admitted to the stroke unit with right arm and face weakness. She follows spoken commands such as 'close your eyes and lift your left hand' correctly, but when asked about her family she produces only a few slow, halting words with great effort and becomes visibly frustrated. She cannot repeat a short phrase. Which brain area is most likely damaged?
why_correct: Non-fluent, effortful, halting speech with preserved comprehension and awareness of the deficit indicates expressive (Broca) aphasia. It results from damage to the inferior frontal gyrus of the dominant, usually left, hemisphere, which fits her right-sided face and arm weakness. Repetition is also impaired because speech production is affected.
why_wrong: A. Wernicke aphasia causes fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension. C. Arcuate fasciculus damage causes conduction aphasia, with fluent speech and good comprehension but poor repetition. D. Right parietal damage in a right-handed person causes neglect rather than aphasia. E. Cerebellar damage causes slurred, ataxic speech (dysarthria), not a language disorder.
pearl: Broca's is broken speech: non-fluent and effortful but with good understanding and insight. Wernicke's is fluent speech with poor understanding.
thinking: Right-sided weakness = left hemisphere ↓ understands commands ↓ slow, effortful, halting speech with frustration ↓ expressive, non-fluent aphasia with intact comprehension ↓ Broca area
exam_trap: C, Arcuate fasciculus — impaired repetition tempts towards conduction aphasia, but conduction aphasia has fluent speech, whereas her speech is slow and effortful.
takeaway: Non-fluent effortful speech with preserved comprehension localises to Broca area.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15259). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: An 83-year-old man is seen in a falls clinic after two falls in a month, both soon after getting out of bed. He feels lightheaded and his vision greys out when he stands up. His blood pressure drops considerably when he moves from lying to standing. His regular medicines include atorvastatin, omeprazole, alendronic acid, paracetamol, amlodipine and doxazosin, the last of which was started recently. Which group of his medicines is most likely contributing to his falls?
why_correct: Postural lightheadedness and falls with a significant drop in blood pressure on standing in an older adult are commonly caused or worsened by antihypertensive medications. Alpha-blockers such as doxazosin and calcium channel blockers impair the normal vasoconstrictor response to standing. A structured medication review to reduce or stop these drugs is an important part of falls prevention.
why_wrong: A. Statins can cause muscle symptoms but do not lower blood pressure on standing. C. Proton pump inhibitors are linked with fractures and low magnesium, not postural hypotension. D. Bisphosphonates reduce fracture risk and do not cause postural hypotension. E. Paracetamol does not affect blood pressure.
pearl: In any older person who falls, measure lying and standing blood pressure and review medicines. Alpha-blockers, diuretics, vasodilators and other antihypertensives are common contributors.
thinking: Older man with falls after standing ↓ lightheadedness and visual greying out ↓ significant postural drop in blood pressure ↓ recently started alpha-blocker alongside a calcium channel blocker ↓ Antihypertensive medications
exam_trap: D, Bisphosphonates — they are linked with falls clinics because they protect against fractures, but they treat the consequence of falls rather than causing the postural blood pressure drop.
takeaway: Postural hypotension and falls in older adults: review antihypertensives, especially alpha-blockers.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN8422). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 74-year-old woman on the surgical ward, two days after a bowel resection, is reviewed urgently by the night doctor. She is grey, clammy and drowsy, and her blood pressure is 76/40 mmHg. The cardiac monitor shows a narrow-complex tachycardia with a chaotic baseline, no visible P waves and varying R–R intervals. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.E: Intravenous amiodarone before any shock is attempted

why_correct: This is atrial fibrillation with adverse features: shock and a reduced conscious level. In a tachyarrhythmia with adverse features, Resuscitation Council UK guidance is synchronised DC cardioversion under sedation or anaesthesia, which restores rhythm faster and more reliably than any drug. Amiodarone is added if the shocks do not work.
why_wrong: B. Oral beta-blockade is too slow, and its negative inotropic effect is unsafe when she is already shocked. C. Digoxin works slowly and is not a treatment for unstable fast AF. D. Anticoagulation matters for stroke prevention but does nothing for the instability. E. Amiodarone is given after shocks that have not worked, not instead of cardioversion in a patient who is shocked.
pearl: Adverse features in tachyarrhythmia are shock, syncope, myocardial ischaemia and heart failure; any one of them moves treatment from drugs to synchronised cardioversion.
thinking: Post-operative patient with irregular narrow-complex tachycardia ↓ hypotension, clamminess and drowsiness = adverse features ↓ unstable tachyarrhythmia needs the fastest, most reliable treatment ↓ Synchronised DC cardioversion
exam_trap: E, intravenous amiodarone — it feels safer than a shock, but in a shocked patient it is reserved for after cardioversion has not worked.
takeaway: AF with shock or a reduced conscious level needs synchronised cardioversion first, not rate-control drugs.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ1126). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 58-year-old woman with diabetic nephropathy has been under the renal clinic for several years, and her kidney function has fallen steadily. She now complains of aching in her hips and lower back. Her latest bloods show a low-normal calcium, a raised phosphate and a raised parathyroid hormone. Which process best explains these results?
why_correct: Failing kidneys retain phosphate and make less active vitamin D (calcitriol), which reduces calcium absorption and tends to lower serum calcium. The parathyroid glands respond by producing more PTH, which is secondary hyperparathyroidism. Over time this causes renal bone disease and bone pain.
why_wrong: A. Primary hyperparathyroidism gives a high calcium with a low or normal phosphate, the opposite of this pattern. C. Tertiary hyperparathyroidism develops after long-standing secondary disease, once the glands become autonomous, and calcium is then high rather than low-normal. D. Hypoparathyroidism has a low PTH, not a raised one. E. Paget's disease typically causes an isolated raised alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium, phosphate and PTH.
pearl: In hyperparathyroidism, calcium points to the type: high in primary, low or normal in secondary, high in tertiary. In CKD, phosphate is usually raised.
thinking: Progressive CKD ↓ phosphate retention and less calcitriol ↓ calcium driven down, PTH up in response ↓ low-normal calcium, high phosphate, high PTH ↓ Secondary hyperparathyroidism
exam_trap: C, tertiary hyperparathyroidism — the long renal history suggests it, but tertiary disease causes hypercalcaemia, and her calcium is low-normal.
takeaway: CKD with low-normal calcium, high phosphate and high PTH means secondary hyperparathyroidism.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ14909). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 33-year-old woman attends a sexual health clinic after noticing a sore on her vulva while shaving. It has been there for about a week and has never hurt. Examination shows a single clean-based ulcer with a firm, indurated edge on the left labium majus, and there are bilateral rubbery, non-tender inguinal lymph nodes. Which infection is the most likely cause?
why_correct: A single painless ulcer with an indurated edge and a clean base, together with non-tender rubbery regional lymph nodes, is the chancre of primary syphilis caused by Treponema pallidum. Because it does not hurt it is easily missed. Diagnosis is by serology, with dark-ground microscopy or PCR of the lesion where available, and she should have a full STI screen.
why_wrong: A. Genital herpes causes multiple painful vesicles or shallow ulcers, often with tender nodes. B. Chancroid causes painful, ragged ulcers with tender, sometimes suppurating, nodes. C. In lymphogranuloma venereum the ulcer is small and short-lived, and the main feature is painful, matted inguinal lymphadenopathy. E. Candidiasis causes itching, soreness and discharge rather than an indurated ulcer.
pearl: Pain helps tell genital ulcers apart: herpes and chancroid hurt, the syphilitic chancre does not. Test anyone with a genital ulcer for syphilis, even if herpes seems more likely.
thinking: Single genital ulcer, present a week ↓ painless with an indurated edge and clean base ↓ non-tender rubbery inguinal nodes ↓ Primary syphilis
exam_trap: A, genital herpes — it is the commonest cause of genital ulceration in the UK, but it hurts and usually gives multiple lesions.
takeaway: A single painless indurated genital ulcer with non-tender nodes is primary syphilis until proven otherwise.

stem: A 49-year-old man comes to the emergency department on crutches the morning after a wedding reception. Overnight the joint at the base of his left great toe became so tender that he could not bear to pull a sock over it. The joint is swollen, and the skin over it is shiny and dusky red. He is afebrile and otherwise well, with no history of injury. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Sudden overnight onset of severe pain, swelling and shiny red skin over the first metatarsophalangeal joint, after an evening of likely heavy eating and drinking, is the classic picture of acute gout. The first MTP joint is the commonest site of a first attack. Joint aspiration for crystals confirms it, but the clinical picture here is typical.
why_wrong: B. Septic arthritis must be considered in any hot joint, but it usually affects a systemically unwell patient and the first MTP joint is an uncommon site. C. Cellulitis causes spreading redness of the skin and soft tissue rather than pain centred on the joint itself. D. Hallux valgus causes chronic deformity and pressure pain, not an acute inflammatory attack overnight. E. Calcium pyrophosphate disease mainly affects the knee and wrist of older adults.
pearl: Alcohol, particularly beer, and purine-rich meals can trigger acute gout; colchicine or an NSAID started early shortens the attack.
thinking: Sudden overnight acute monoarthritis ↓ first MTP joint, exquisite tenderness, shiny red skin ↓ heavy food and alcohol intake, afebrile and well ↓ Gout
exam_trap: B, septic arthritis — the joint is hot and exquisitely tender, but he is afebrile and well and the site is classic for gout; aspirate if any doubt remains.
takeaway: Sudden, exquisitely painful swelling of the big toe joint in a well man is acute gout until shown otherwise.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15149). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit having taken an overdose the previous evening. She has vomited repeatedly, is sweaty, and describes a constant buzzing in her ears with muffled hearing. A venous blood gas shows a metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap. Which drug did she most likely take?
why_correct: Vomiting, sweating, tinnitus with reduced hearing and a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis after an overdose point to aspirin. Salicylates disrupt cellular metabolism, producing acid, and directly affect the inner ear. A salicylate level guides treatment such as urinary alkalinisation or haemodialysis in severe cases.
why_wrong: A. Amitriptyline causes drowsiness, anticholinergic signs, seizures and arrhythmias rather than tinnitus. B. Paracetamol causes delayed liver injury and does not cause tinnitus. C. Iron causes vomiting and acidosis but not tinnitus or hearing change. D. Lithium toxicity causes tremor, ataxia and confusion rather than tinnitus with acidosis.
pearl: Tinnitus or deafness after an overdose should prompt a salicylate level, even when the patient does not name the drug taken.
thinking: Overdose with repeated vomiting ↓ tinnitus and muffled hearing ↓ raised anion gap metabolic acidosis ↓ combination fits salicylate toxicity ↓ Aspirin
exam_trap: C, Iron sulfate — iron overdose also causes vomiting and a metabolic acidosis, but it does not affect hearing, which is the discriminating clue.
takeaway: Overdose with vomiting, acidosis and ear symptoms suggests aspirin: check a salicylate level.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ14832). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 66-year-old woman has taken omeprazole for heartburn for many years. Over the past six weeks, food has begun sticking behind her breastbone, first with meat and now with bread. She has lost a little weight. Examination is unremarkable. Which next step is most appropriate?

options.A: Double the omeprazole dose and review in eight weeks
options.D: Refer to speech and language therapy
options.E: Advise a soft diet and reassure

why_correct: New, progressive dysphagia to solids is an alarm symptom that needs urgent endoscopy to exclude oesophageal cancer or a peptic stricture. NICE suspected cancer guidance recommends urgent direct-access upper GI endoscopy for dysphagia. Long-standing reflux increases the risk of Barrett's oesophagus and adenocarcinoma.
why_wrong: A. Increasing acid suppression delays the diagnosis of a potentially serious cause. B. H. pylori testing is for dyspepsia without alarm features. D. Speech and language therapy assesses oropharyngeal swallowing, whereas food sticking behind the sternum suggests an oesophageal cause. E. Reassurance without investigation risks missing cancer.
pearl: Dysphagia at any age is an alarm symptom needing urgent endoscopy. Progression from solids to softer foods suggests a mechanical narrowing.
thinking: Long-standing reflux ↓ new dysphagia behind the sternum ↓ progressive, with weight loss ↓ alarm features for cancer or stricture ↓ Urgent upper GI endoscopy
exam_trap: A, Double the omeprazole dose — it is a common step for persistent reflux, but new dysphagia is an alarm symptom that needs investigation, not more acid suppression.
takeaway: New dysphagia in long-standing reflux needs urgent endoscopy.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAAKT039). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 64-year-old woman attends the emergency department with 40 minutes of heavy upper abdominal and lower chest discomfort, nausea and sweating. Her heart rate is 52 beats/min. Her ECG shows ST elevation in lead III that is greater than in lead II, with ST elevation also in aVF and reciprocal ST depression in leads I and aVL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: ST elevation in II, III and aVF reflects injury to the inferior wall of the left ventricle, and reciprocal depression in I and aVL supports an acute infarct. The inferior wall is usually supplied by the right coronary artery, which also supplies the sinoatrial and atrioventricular nodes, explaining the bradycardia. Inferior infarction often presents with epigastric discomfort and nausea, and needs immediate reperfusion.
why_wrong: A. Anterior STEMI causes ST elevation in the chest leads V1 to V4. B. Lateral STEMI causes ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6, where there is depression here. C. Pericarditis causes widespread concave ST elevation without reciprocal depression. D. Posterior infarction causes ST depression in V1 to V3 rather than inferior ST elevation.
pearl: Inferior STEMI: ST elevation in II, III and aVF. Look for right ventricular involvement (right-sided leads) and bradycardia, and be cautious with nitrates if the right ventricle is involved.
thinking: Epigastric and lower chest discomfort with sweating ↓ bradycardia ↓ ST elevation in III, II and aVF ↓ reciprocal depression in I and aVL ↓ Inferior STEMI
exam_trap: C, Acute pericarditis — ST elevation across several leads can suggest it, but pericarditis is widespread and lacks reciprocal ST depression.
takeaway: ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal change in I and aVL means inferior STEMI.

stem: A 61-year-old woman who smokes describes a cramping ache in both buttocks and thighs whenever she walks uphill to the shops. It always starts at about the same point and goes within a couple of minutes if she simply stands still; she does not need to sit down or lean forward for relief. Her femoral pulses are weak on both sides. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.E: Intermittent claudication due to peripheral arterial disease

correct_answer: E. Intermittent claudication due to peripheral arterial disease
why_correct: Reproducible exercise-induced cramping that settles promptly with standing still reflects muscle ischaemia from peripheral arterial disease. Buttock and thigh symptoms with weak femoral pulses suggest aortoiliac disease. She needs ankle brachial pressure index measurement, smoking cessation, an antiplatelet and statin, and a supervised exercise programme.
why_wrong: A. Spinal stenosis causes neurogenic claudication that is relieved by sitting or bending forward, not by simply standing still. B. Hip osteoarthritis causes groin pain related to joint movement and stiffness rather than reproducible exertional cramping. C. DVT causes persistent unilateral leg swelling and pain. D. Sciatica causes radiating pain below the knee that is not reliably relieved by standing still.
pearl: Vascular claudication eases on standing still; neurogenic claudication needs sitting or bending forward. Always check the pulses.
thinking: Smoker with exertional buttock and thigh cramp ↓ reproducible distance ↓ relieved by standing still ↓ weak femoral pulses ↓ Intermittent claudication from peripheral arterial disease
exam_trap: A, Lumbar spinal stenosis — it causes exertional buttock and leg pain in older adults, but relief requires sitting or bending forward and the pulses are normal.
takeaway: Exertional leg cramp relieved by standing still with weak pulses means arterial claudication.

stem: A 79-year-old woman is found to have an irregularly irregular pulse at a routine GP review, and an ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. Her heart rate is already controlled on bisoprolol. After assessing her risks, the GP recommends starting a direct oral anticoagulant, and she asks what this new tablet will do for her. Which best describes why this treatment is offered?

options.B: To convert her heart back to a normal rhythm
options.D: To reduce her risk of stroke from clots forming in the heart

correct_answer: D. To reduce her risk of stroke from clots forming in the heart
why_correct: In atrial fibrillation, ineffective atrial contraction allows blood to stagnate, especially in the left atrial appendage, where clots can form and travel to the brain. Anticoagulation substantially reduces this risk of embolic stroke. Its benefit is weighed against bleeding risk, using tools recommended by NICE.
why_wrong: A. Rate control is achieved with beta-blockers, rate-limiting calcium channel blockers or digoxin. B. Rhythm control requires cardioversion or antiarrhythmic drugs. C. Anticoagulants have no meaningful effect on blood pressure. E. Preventing myocardial infarction is not the purpose of anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation.
pearl: In AF, rate or rhythm control treats symptoms, while anticoagulation prevents stroke. They are separate decisions and both should be considered.
thinking: New atrial fibrillation ↓ rate already controlled ↓ atrial stasis allows clot formation ↓ clots can embolise to the brain ↓ Anticoagulation reduces stroke risk
exam_trap: B, Convert her heart back to a normal rhythm — patients and candidates often assume the new AF tablet treats the rhythm, but anticoagulants do not affect rhythm.
takeaway: Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation is given to prevent embolic stroke.

stem: A 64-year-old woman attends her GP because she now has to stop for breath halfway up the hill to the shops. She has had a morning cough with small amounts of clear sputum for several winters and needed antibiotics twice last year for chest infections. She smoked 20 cigarettes a day for 40 years and stopped last year. There is no history of childhood wheeze or hay fever. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows an obstructive pattern with only a small change after salbutamol. Which condition best accounts for her symptoms?
why_correct: Progressive exertional breathlessness and a chronic productive cough in a long-term smoker, with airflow obstruction that persists after a bronchodilator, is COPD. The minimal bronchodilator response and lack of atopic history point away from asthma. Management includes smoking cessation support, pulmonary rehabilitation where appropriate, vaccinations and inhaled therapy.
why_wrong: A. Asthma usually shows variable symptoms and marked bronchodilator reversibility, often with an atopic history. B. Bronchiectasis causes daily copious purulent sputum and is confirmed on CT, not suggested by small amounts of clear sputum. C. Heart failure causes breathlessness with orthopnoea and oedema, not fixed airflow obstruction on spirometry. E. Pulmonary fibrosis causes a restrictive pattern with fine inspiratory crackles, not obstruction.
pearl: COPD is diagnosed clinically in a person with risk factors and confirmed by post-bronchodilator spirometry showing airflow obstruction; a large bronchodilator response should make you reconsider asthma.
thinking: Long-term smoker in middle age ↓ chronic morning cough, recurrent winter infections and progressive exertional breathlessness ↓ obstructive spirometry with little bronchodilator response ↓ no atopic or childhood history ↓ COPD
exam_trap: A, Asthma — obstructive spirometry and wheezy chest infections tempt towards asthma, but the persistent obstruction after salbutamol, heavy smoking history and lack of atopy fit COPD.
takeaway: Persistent post-bronchodilator airflow obstruction in a long-term smoker with chronic cough and breathlessness is COPD.

stem: A 33-year-old man who injects heroin presents to the emergency department with a week of fevers and night sweats. He has a new pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge. He is alert, his blood pressure and heart rate are stable, and there are no signs of shock. The team suspects infective endocarditis. Which step must come before antibiotics are given?

options.A: Start empirical intravenous antibiotics without delay
options.B: Arrange echocardiography and wait for the report
options.C: Request a CT scan of the chest
options.D: Take several sets of blood cultures from separate venepuncture sites

correct_answer: D. Take several sets of blood cultures from separate venepuncture sites
why_correct: In a haemodynamically stable patient with suspected infective endocarditis, several sets of blood cultures should be taken from separate sites before antibiotics, because prior antibiotics can prevent identification of the organism and its sensitivities. Identifying the organism guides the choice and duration of therapy. In people who inject drugs the tricuspid valve is commonly affected, often by Staphylococcus aureus.
why_wrong: A. Immediate antibiotics before cultures are reserved for patients who are septic or unstable, and he is stable. B. Echocardiography is essential but should not come before or delay blood cultures. C. CT chest may show septic emboli but is not the priority before treatment. E. Anticoagulation does not treat endocarditis and may increase bleeding risk if there are emboli.
pearl: Tricuspid endocarditis in people who inject drugs causes a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge and may present with septic pulmonary emboli.
thinking: Person who injects drugs with fever and night sweats ↓ new pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge ↓ suspected endocarditis, haemodynamically stable ↓ organism identification guides prolonged therapy ↓ Take several sets of blood cultures from separate venepuncture sites
exam_trap: A, Start empirical intravenous antibiotics without delay — sepsis teaching tempts towards immediate antibiotics, but in a stable patient with suspected endocarditis, cultures taken first allow the organism to be identified.
takeaway: In stable suspected endocarditis, take multiple blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics.

stem: A 41-year-old man was diagnosed with coeliac disease on duodenal biopsy 18 months ago. He tells his GP he still has bloating and loose stools most weeks. His IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody level fell after diagnosis but remains above the normal range. He eats out at work most lunchtimes. What should be done first?

options.B: Review his gluten intake with a specialist dietitian

correct_answer: B. Review his gluten intake with a specialist dietitian
why_correct: The commonest reason for persistent symptoms in treated coeliac disease is continued gluten exposure, often inadvertent through cross-contamination or eating out. A persistently raised tTG antibody supports ongoing gluten intake. A detailed dietary review with a specialist dietitian is the first step before investigating other causes or refractory disease.
why_wrong: A. Colonoscopy may be considered for other causes such as microscopic colitis, but only after dietary adherence is checked. C. Steroids are reserved for confirmed refractory coeliac disease under specialist care. D. Repeat biopsy is considered if symptoms persist despite confirmed strict adherence. E. Pancreatic insufficiency is a less common cause and is investigated after gluten exposure has been addressed.
pearl: Coeliac serology falls on a strict gluten-free diet and is useful for monitoring adherence; persistently raised antibodies usually mean ongoing gluten exposure.
thinking: Established coeliac disease ↓ persistent bloating and loose stools ↓ tTG still raised and frequently eats out ↓ ongoing gluten exposure is the commonest cause ↓ Review his gluten intake with a specialist dietitian
exam_trap: D, Repeat the duodenal biopsy — persistent symptoms tempt towards re-examining the gut, but checking for dietary gluten comes first, especially when antibodies remain raised.
takeaway: Persistent symptoms in treated coeliac disease mean checking gluten-free diet adherence first.

presentation: Refusal Of Treatment By A Patient With Capacity
stem: A 54-year-old man on the surgical ward has had several admissions with gallstone pain and is offered a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. After a full discussion he declines surgery. He can explain the likely risks of further attacks, weighs them against his fear of operations and gives a consistent answer on two occasions. His wife is upset and asks the team to go ahead anyway. Which is the most appropriate course of action?

options.A: Ask his wife to sign the consent form on his behalf
options.B: Respect his decision, document the discussion and keep the option open
options.C: Proceed with surgery in his best interests
options.D: Apply to the Court of Protection to authorise surgery
options.E: Delay his discharge until he agrees to the operation

correct_answer: B. Respect his decision, document the discussion and keep the option open
why_correct: An adult with capacity can refuse treatment, even when the decision seems unwise to the team. The doctor should ensure he has the information he needs, document the discussion and his capacity, explain the warning signs that should prompt him to seek help, and make clear that he can change his mind. Relatives cannot consent for an adult who has capacity.
why_wrong: A. Relatives have no authority to consent for an adult with capacity. C. Best-interests decisions apply only when a patient lacks capacity. D. Court involvement is not needed when a capacitous adult has made a clear decision. E. Holding him in hospital to coerce agreement is unlawful and unethical.
pearl: Capacity is decision-specific and presumed in adults. An unwise decision is not proof of incapacity, and a capacitous refusal must be respected.
thinking: Adult offered elective surgery ↓ understands, retains, weighs and communicates his choice ↓ has capacity for this decision ↓ capacitous refusal is binding ↓ Respect his decision, document the discussion and keep the option open
exam_trap: C, Proceed with surgery in his best interests — it tempts because the team believes surgery would help, but best interests apply only to a person who lacks capacity, which he does not.
takeaway: An adult with capacity may refuse treatment; respect it, document it and leave the door open.

stem: An 18-year-old woman visits her practice nurse before moving into university halls of residence. Her records show she was absent from school on the day of the Year 9 meningococcal immunisation and has never had it since. She is otherwise fully immunised. She asks which vaccine will protect her against the meningococcal groups covered by the routine teenage programme. Which vaccine should be offered?
why_correct: The routine UK adolescent programme includes the MenACWY conjugate vaccine, which protects against meningococcal groups A, C, W and Y and reduces carriage in teenagers. Those who missed it remain eligible for a catch-up dose up to their 25th birthday, and first-time university entrants are specifically encouraged to have it. She should be offered MenACWY now.
why_wrong: A. MenB vaccine is given in the infant programme and does not protect against groups A, C, W or Y. B. Hib/MenC covers only group C, and is not the adolescent vaccine. C. HPV vaccine protects against human papillomavirus, not meningococcal disease. E. Pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine protects against pneumococcus and is used mainly for older and at-risk groups.
pearl: MenACWY is the routine teenage meningococcal vaccine, and people who missed it can catch up until their 25th birthday. Encourage it before university.
thinking: Teenager who missed the school meningococcal dose ↓ moving into shared university accommodation ↓ adolescent vaccine covers groups A, C, W and Y ↓ catch-up eligibility applies ↓ MenACWY conjugate vaccine
exam_trap: A, MenB vaccine — it tempts because group B is an important cause of meningococcal disease, but MenB is part of the infant schedule and does not cover the groups in the adolescent programme.
takeaway: Missed the teenage meningococcal dose? Offer MenACWY catch-up, especially before university.

presentation: Contraception For A Competent Young Person
stem: A 15-year-old girl attends her GP alone and asks to start the contraceptive pill. She is in a relationship with a boyfriend of similar age and says the relationship is consensual, with no signs of pressure or exploitation. She understands the benefits, risks and how to take the pill, but despite encouragement she does not want her parents to know. She is likely to continue having sex without contraception. Which is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Refuse to prescribe without parental consent
options.B: Prescribe, but inform her parents after the consultation
options.C: Advise her to return when she reaches 16
options.D: Provide contraception confidentially, having assessed her competence and the Fraser criteria
options.E: Make a safeguarding referral for all sexual activity under 16

correct_answer: D. Provide contraception confidentially, having assessed her competence and the Fraser criteria
why_correct: Young people under 16 can consent to their own treatment if they have sufficient maturity and understanding (Gillick competence). For contraception, the Fraser guidelines also apply: she understands the advice, cannot be persuaded to involve her parents, is likely to continue having sex, her health may suffer without contraception, and treatment is in her best interests. Confidentiality should be respected, while remaining alert to safeguarding concerns such as exploitation or a large age gap.
why_wrong: A. Parental consent is not required for a competent young person meeting the Fraser criteria. B. Informing her parents breaches confidentiality without justification. C. Delaying contraception exposes her to the risk of unplanned pregnancy. E. Sexual activity at this age does not automatically require referral when there are no safeguarding concerns, though every case needs assessment.
pearl: Under 16s can consent to contraception if Gillick competent and the Fraser criteria are met. Always assess for exploitation, and note that sexual activity under 13 always requires safeguarding action.
thinking: Young person under 16 requesting contraception ↓ understands and weighs the information ↓ declines parental involvement, will continue sex ↓ no safeguarding concerns identified ↓ Provide contraception confidentially, having assessed her competence and the Fraser criteria
exam_trap: E, Make a safeguarding referral for all sexual activity under 16 — it tempts because she is under the age of consent, but referral depends on an individual risk assessment, and a consensual relationship with a peer of similar age without exploitation does not automatically need one.
takeaway: A competent under-16 meeting the Fraser criteria can receive confidential contraception.

stem: A 71-year-old woman is brought by ambulance to the emergency department 50 minutes after her husband saw her slump at the breakfast table. She has a left facial droop, cannot lift her left arm and her speech is slurred. Her capillary glucose is normal. Thrombolysis and thrombectomy are being considered. Which investigation is needed immediately?
correct_answer: C. Non-contrast CT of the head
why_correct: Sudden focal neurological deficit within the treatment window needs immediate brain imaging, usually a non-contrast CT head, to exclude intracerebral haemorrhage before any reperfusion treatment. Hypoglycaemia, a key stroke mimic, has already been excluded. CT angiography is added when thrombectomy is being considered.
why_wrong: A. Carotid imaging is part of the later work-up for secondary prevention, not the first test. B. Echocardiography looks for a cardiac source of embolism after the acute phase. D. Ambulatory ECG to detect atrial fibrillation is a later investigation. E. Lumbar puncture has no role in acute stroke and is contraindicated before imaging.
pearl: Time is brain: check glucose, then image immediately. Reperfusion treatment can never be given until a scan has excluded bleeding.
thinking: Sudden unilateral face and arm weakness with dysarthria ↓ Within the reperfusion window ↓ Glucose normal, mimic excluded ↓ Must exclude haemorrhage before treatment ↓ Immediate non-contrast CT head
exam_trap: A, carotid duplex ultrasound — carotid disease is a common cause of stroke, but carotid imaging guides later prevention and must not delay the CT that decides on reperfusion.
takeaway: In suspected acute stroke, image the brain immediately to exclude bleeding before reperfusion.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ11374). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 58-year-old man attends the emergency department with a painful, swollen left leg. He had a knee arthroscopy 10 days ago and has spent most of the time since on the sofa. His left calf is visibly larger than the right, with pitting oedema and tenderness along the deep veins. He has no chest symptoms. A clinical prediction score indicates that DVT is likely. Which investigation should be arranged?

options.B: D-dimer, with imaging only if the result is raised

why_correct: When DVT is likely on a clinical prediction score, NICE recommends a proximal leg vein ultrasound, ideally within a few hours. If the scan cannot be done promptly, a D-dimer is taken and interim anticoagulation started while waiting. Recent surgery and immobility are strong provoking factors here.
why_wrong: B. Starting with a D-dimer is the pathway when DVT is unlikely; a negative result cannot safely exclude DVT when clinical probability is high. C. CTPA investigates pulmonary embolism and he has no chest symptoms. D. ABPI assesses arterial disease, not venous thrombosis. E. A knee radiograph does not show a venous clot.
pearl: The clinical probability decides the first test: likely DVT goes straight to ultrasound, unlikely DVT starts with a D-dimer. A positive D-dimer is non-specific, especially after surgery.
thinking: Unilateral leg swelling with deep vein tenderness ↓ Recent surgery and immobility ↓ Prediction score says DVT likely ↓ D-dimer cannot rule it out at this probability ↓ Proximal leg vein ultrasound
exam_trap: B, D-dimer first — it is the familiar first step, but D-dimer is a rule-out test for low-probability patients; with a likely DVT and recent surgery it adds nothing and delays diagnosis.
takeaway: Likely DVT goes straight to proximal leg ultrasound; D-dimer first only when DVT is unlikely.

stem: A 54-year-old man with diabetic kidney disease, who takes ramipril and spironolactone, is brought to the emergency department feeling weak and light-headed. A venous blood gas shows a dangerously high potassium, and his ECG shows broad QRS complexes with absent P waves. Which treatment should be given first?
why_correct: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is an emergency because of the risk of fatal arrhythmia. Intravenous calcium stabilises the cardiac membrane within minutes; it does not lower potassium but protects the heart while other treatments act. It is followed by insulin with glucose to shift potassium into cells, removal of the causative drugs and measures to remove potassium from the body.
why_wrong: A. Insulin with glucose lowers potassium but should follow calcium when the ECG is abnormal. B. Salbutamol is an add-on to shift potassium and does not protect the myocardium. C. Potassium binders act over hours and are not an emergency first step. D. Furosemide has a limited, slow effect and does not protect the heart.
pearl: Remember the order: protect the heart with calcium, shift potassium into cells with insulin and glucose, then remove potassium from the body, and stop the drugs that caused it.
thinking: Kidney disease plus ACE inhibitor and spironolactone ↓ Very high potassium ↓ Broad QRS, absent P waves ↓ Risk of arrhythmia ↓ Stabilise the myocardium with IV calcium first
exam_trap: A, insulin with glucose — it is the most effective way to lower potassium quickly, but with ECG changes the heart must be protected first with calcium.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: give IV calcium first to protect the heart, then lower potassium.

stem: An 84-year-old man who lives alone is seen at home by his GP after his third fall in two months. His medicines include amlodipine, doxazosin, furosemide, amitriptyline for nerve pain and zopiclone at night, along with several others. He feels light-headed when he gets up, and his blood pressure drops on standing. He has no injury today. What should the GP do first?

options.B: Stop all his regular medicines today
options.C: Carry out a structured medication review aimed at reducing falls-risk drugs
options.D: Arrange a CT scan of the head

correct_answer: C. Carry out a structured medication review aimed at reducing falls-risk drugs
why_correct: Several of his medicines can cause postural hypotension or sedation, both major contributors to falls in older people. A structured medication review identifies which drugs to reduce or stop safely, such as the alpha-blocker, sedatives and the tricyclic. This is a key part of a multifactorial falls assessment.
why_wrong: A. Adding fludrocortisone treats the symptom with another drug rather than removing the cause. B. Stopping all medicines at once risks rebound effects and loss of needed treatment. D. He has no head injury or neurological signs needing a CT scan. E. Care home placement is not the first step when a reversible cause is likely.
pearl: Common falls-risk drugs in older people include alpha-blockers, antihypertensives, diuretics, sedatives, tricyclics, antipsychotics and opioids; deprescribing is often the most effective intervention.
thinking: Older man with recurrent falls ↓ Multiple drugs causing sedation and low blood pressure ↓ Postural drop confirmed ↓ Medication is the likely reversible cause ↓ Structured medication review
exam_trap: A, start fludrocortisone — it can treat postural hypotension, but adding a drug when the cause is medication burden is a prescribing cascade; deprescribing comes first.
takeaway: Recurrent falls on many medicines call for a structured medication review before adding anything.

stem: A 74-year-old woman develops sudden severe mid-back pain while bending to lift a bag of shopping. She has had no fall or other injury. A spinal X-ray shows a wedge compression fracture of the T12 vertebra. She has no weight loss or night sweats, and her full blood count, calcium, ESR and serum protein electrophoresis are all normal. Which underlying condition is most likely?
why_correct: A vertebral compression fracture from minimal stress, such as bending or lifting, in an older woman is a fragility fracture, and osteoporosis is the most likely cause. Normal blood count, calcium, ESR and protein electrophoresis make malignancy unlikely. She should have a fracture risk assessment with DXA scanning and be considered for bone-protective treatment, calcium and vitamin D.
why_wrong: A. Myeloma can cause vertebral collapse, but normal blood count, calcium, ESR and electrophoresis make it unlikely. B. Osteomalacia causes bone pain, muscle weakness and abnormal calcium, phosphate or vitamin D. C. Metastases are unlikely with no cancer history, no systemic features and normal bloods. D. Paget disease causes bone pain and deformity with a raised alkaline phosphatase, not typical wedge fractures.
pearl: Many vertebral fragility fractures are found incidentally or dismissed as back strain; a vertebral fracture strongly predicts future hip and wrist fractures.
thinking: Older woman with minimal-trauma vertebral fracture ↓ fragility fracture ↓ normal FBC, calcium, ESR, electrophoresis ↓ malignancy unlikely ↓ osteoporosis, arrange DXA and bone protection
exam_trap: A, multiple myeloma — it is a classic cause of vertebral collapse in older people, but the normal blood count, calcium, ESR and electrophoresis argue strongly against it.
takeaway: A low-trauma fracture in an older adult is a fragility fracture; assess for osteoporosis.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15541). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Child disclosure with a request for secrecy
stem: A 13-year-old boy attends a GP appointment about a sports injury. Towards the end, he says his father often hits him with a belt when angry, and he asks the GP to promise not to tell anyone because he is afraid of what might happen. What is the most appropriate response?

options.A: Promise to keep it secret so that he continues to trust the GP
options.B: Ask his father to attend to discuss the allegation
options.C: Advise him to tell a teacher instead
options.D: Explain that you cannot keep this secret and act on safeguarding procedures
options.E: Document the disclosure and review him in a month

correct_answer: D. Explain that you cannot keep this secret and act on safeguarding procedures
why_correct: A disclosure of physical abuse is a safeguarding concern, and the child's safety outweighs a request for confidentiality. The GP should not promise secrecy, but should explain kindly what will happen next and share information with the appropriate safeguarding team or children's social care, following local procedures. Involving the child in the process as far as possible helps maintain trust.
why_wrong: A. Promising secrecy may leave him at risk and is a promise the doctor cannot keep. B. Confronting the alleged abuser first may increase the risk to the child. C. Passing responsibility to someone else does not discharge the doctor's own safeguarding duty. E. Delaying action leaves him exposed to ongoing harm.
pearl: Never promise a child total confidentiality; explain that you may need to share information to keep them safe and follow local safeguarding procedures.
thinking: Child discloses physical abuse ↓ Asks for secrecy ↓ Child's safety takes priority ↓ Confidentiality not absolute in safeguarding ↓ Explain you cannot keep it secret and act
exam_trap: A, promising secrecy — preserving trust feels important, but it may leave the child at risk and the doctor cannot honour it.
takeaway: A child's safety overrides their request for secrecy; follow safeguarding procedures.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15077). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Dry mouth, dry eyes and parotid swelling
stem: A 52-year-old woman tells her GP that her eyes feel gritty all the time, she needs a drink of water to swallow dry food such as crackers, and she keeps a glass by her bed at night. Over the past year she has had several bouts of tender swelling in front of both ears. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Persistent dry eyes and dry mouth with recurrent parotid swelling in a middle-aged woman are characteristic of Sjögren syndrome, an autoimmune disease of the exocrine glands. Investigations include anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies and specialist rheumatology assessment. It also carries an increased risk of lymphoma, so persistent gland enlargement needs review.
why_wrong: A. Mumps causes an acute, self-limiting parotitis with fever rather than chronic dryness and recurrent episodes. B. Systemic sclerosis mainly causes skin thickening, Raynaud phenomenon and organ fibrosis. C. A salivary stone causes unilateral swelling with meals and does not cause dry eyes. E. Rheumatoid arthritis can be associated with secondary Sjögren syndrome but would present with inflammatory joint disease.
pearl: Dry eyes plus dry mouth with parotid swelling suggests Sjögren syndrome; check anti-Ro and anti-La and remember the increased lymphoma risk.
thinking: Middle-aged woman ↓ Gritty dry eyes and dry mouth ↓ Recurrent bilateral parotid swelling ↓ Autoimmune exocrine gland disease ↓ Sjögren syndrome
exam_trap: C, salivary gland calculus — gland swelling suggests obstruction, but a stone is usually unilateral, meal-related and does not cause dry eyes.
takeaway: Chronic dry eyes and dry mouth with parotid swelling point to Sjögren syndrome.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15920). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 64-year-old man with stage 4 chronic kidney disease is reviewed in the renal clinic for increasing tiredness. His haemoglobin has fallen to a low level with a normal mean cell volume. His ferritin, transferrin saturation, vitamin B12 and folate are normal, and there is no evidence of blood loss. Which mechanism most directly explains his anaemia?

options.A: Iron deficiency from occult gastrointestinal loss

why_correct: The kidneys produce erythropoietin, which drives red cell production in the bone marrow. In advanced chronic kidney disease, reduced erythropoietin output causes a normocytic anaemia. Once iron status is optimised, it can be treated with an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent under specialist care.
why_wrong: A. His iron studies are normal and there is no evidence of blood loss. B. Vitamin B12 is normal, and deficiency would usually cause macrocytosis. C. Hypothyroidism can contribute to anaemia but is not the principal mechanism in CKD. E. Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium balance, not red cell production.
pearl: Anaemia of CKD is normocytic and due mainly to erythropoietin deficiency; correct iron deficiency first, as ESAs work poorly without adequate iron.
thinking: Advanced chronic kidney disease ↓ Normocytic anaemia ↓ Iron, B12 and folate normal ↓ Kidneys normally produce erythropoietin ↓ Reduced erythropoietin production
exam_trap: A, occult GI blood loss — iron deficiency is common in CKD and must be excluded, but his iron studies are normal here.
takeaway: Normocytic anaemia in advanced CKD is mainly due to reduced erythropoietin production.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15110). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 38-year-old woman tells her GP that for the past eight months her periods have been so heavy that she floods through pads, passes clots and has to change protection overnight. Her cycle is regular, and she has no bleeding between periods or after sex. Her cervical screening is up to date and abdominal examination is normal. Which investigation should be offered to her routinely?
why_correct: NICE advises that all women presenting with heavy menstrual bleeding should have a full blood count, because chronic blood loss commonly causes iron-deficiency anaemia that may need treatment in its own right. Further tests are guided by the history and examination rather than done routinely. With a regular cycle, no intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding and a normal examination, she may be offered treatment without further investigation.
why_wrong: A. Ultrasound is reserved for women with a suspected structural cause, such as an enlarged uterus or pelvic mass on examination. C. Ferritin is not routinely needed; the full blood count is the recommended first test. D. Thyroid tests are indicated only if there are other features of thyroid disease. E. Coagulation testing is for women with features suggesting a bleeding disorder, such as heavy periods since menarche or other bleeding problems.
pearl: Heavy menstrual bleeding is defined by its impact on a woman's quality of life rather than by measured blood loss; a full blood count is the one routine test.
thinking: Heavy, regular periods with clots and flooding ↓ No intermenstrual or postcoital bleeding, normal examination ↓ Main routine concern is anaemia from blood loss ↓ Full blood count
exam_trap: C, Serum ferritin — iron deficiency is the worry, so measuring iron stores seems logical, but guidance recommends a full blood count for everyone and does not advise routine ferritin testing.
takeaway: Every woman with heavy menstrual bleeding needs a full blood count; other tests depend on the history.
