stem: A 35-year-old man with type 1 diabetes and vitiligo has felt increasingly tired for several months and becomes light-headed when he stands up. He craves salty food and has had several unexplained hypoglycaemic episodes despite reducing his insulin. There is increased pigmentation of his palmar creases and inside his cheeks. His blood pressure falls on standing. Blood tests show low sodium and high potassium. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

why_correct: Fatigue, postural hypotension, salt craving, falling insulin requirements, mucosal and palmar crease pigmentation, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia in a man with other autoimmune conditions are classic features of autoimmune primary adrenal insufficiency. Pigmentation reflects high ACTH, and hyperkalaemia reflects loss of aldosterone. Diagnosis is confirmed with a morning cortisol and a short Synacthen test, and an adrenal crisis must be treated with hydrocortisone without delay.
why_wrong: B. Secondary adrenal insufficiency from hypopituitarism causes pale skin, not pigmentation, and potassium is usually normal because aldosterone is preserved. C. SIADH causes low sodium with euvolaemia, but not hyperkalaemia, postural hypotension or pigmentation. D. Primary hyperaldosteronism causes hypertension and low potassium. E. Hypothyroidism may cause fatigue and low sodium but not pigmentation or hyperkalaemia.
pearl: Recurrent unexplained hypoglycaemia in someone with type 1 diabetes should raise suspicion of coexisting adrenal insufficiency or coeliac disease.
thinking: Autoimmune background with fatigue and postural dizziness ↓ Salt craving, falling insulin needs, pigmentation ↓ Low sodium with high potassium ↓ Addison's disease
exam_trap: B, Hypopituitarism — it also causes cortisol deficiency, but pigmentation and hyperkalaemia point to a primary adrenal problem with high ACTH and loss of aldosterone.
takeaway: Pigmentation, postural hypotension, hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia suggest Addison's disease.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ14747). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Adrenal insufficiency after stopping long-term steroids
stem: A 58-year-old woman with polymyalgia rheumatica has taken prednisolone for ten months. Feeling much better, she stopped her tablets suddenly last week without telling anyone. She now attends the GP with profound fatigue, nausea, loss of appetite and dizziness when she stands. She has no shoulder or hip girdle stiffness. Her blood pressure is low and falls further on standing. Which is the most likely explanation?

options.A: Adrenal insufficiency from suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis

correct_answer: A. Adrenal insufficiency from suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis
why_correct: Prolonged glucocorticoid therapy suppresses ACTH release, and the adrenal glands atrophy and cannot produce enough cortisol when the drug is stopped abruptly. The result is adrenal insufficiency, with fatigue, nausea and hypotension, which can progress to a life-threatening adrenal crisis. Steroids taken for more than a few weeks should be withdrawn gradually, and patients should carry a steroid emergency card and be warned not to stop suddenly.
why_wrong: B. A relapse of polymyalgia would cause recurrent girdle pain and stiffness, which she does not have. C. Steroid-induced hyperglycaemia occurs while taking steroids and improves after stopping them. D. Hypothyroidism develops gradually and is not caused by stopping prednisolone. E. A perforated ulcer causes sudden severe abdominal pain and peritonism.
pearl: Patients on long-term oral steroids should have sick day rules explained and carry a steroid emergency card so that emergency hydrocortisone is not delayed.
thinking: Months of prednisolone ↓ Abrupt self-discontinuation ↓ Fatigue, nausea and postural hypotension without girdle symptoms ↓ Adrenal insufficiency from HPA axis suppression
exam_trap: B, relapse of polymyalgia rheumatica — tempting because symptoms began after stopping treatment, but relapse would bring back girdle pain and stiffness, not nausea and hypotension.
takeaway: Never stop long-term steroids abruptly; HPA suppression can cause adrenal insufficiency and crisis.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15361). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 78-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her daughter because over several days she has become muddled, nauseated and unsteady on her feet. Indapamide was started for hypertension four weeks ago. She has no urinary symptoms and appears clinically euvolaemic. Blood tests show a markedly low sodium and a low potassium; glucose and calcium are normal. Which is the most likely cause?

options.C: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion from lung cancer

why_correct: Thiazide and thiazide-like diuretics such as indapamide impair the kidney's ability to dilute urine and commonly cause hyponatraemia, especially in older women and in the first weeks of treatment. Coexisting hypokalaemia supports a diuretic cause. The drug should be stopped and the sodium corrected cautiously to avoid osmotic demyelination.
why_wrong: A. Addison's disease causes hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia and hypotension, not hypokalaemia. B. Infection can cause delirium in older people, but she has no urinary symptoms and this would not explain the electrolyte pattern. C. SIADH from cancer is possible but less likely than a recently started drug known to cause hyponatraemia. D. Hypothyroidism is an uncommon cause of hyponatraemia and would not explain hypokalaemia.
pearl: Always check sodium and potassium within a few weeks of starting a thiazide or thiazide-like diuretic in an older person.
thinking: Older woman with confusion and unsteadiness ↓ Thiazide-like diuretic started recently ↓ Low sodium with low potassium, euvolaemic ↓ Indapamide-induced hyponatraemia
exam_trap: B, urinary tract infection with delirium — tempting because infection is a common cause of confusion in older people, but there are no urinary symptoms and the electrolytes point to the new diuretic.
takeaway: New confusion soon after starting a thiazide-like diuretic: check sodium and suspect drug-induced hyponatraemia.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15208). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 59-year-old woman attends her GP for a blood pressure review. Amlodipine was started two months ago. Since then both ankles become puffy by the evening, improving overnight. She has no breathlessness on exertion or lying flat. Her jugular venous pressure is not raised, her chest is clear, her calves are soft and non-tender, and urine dipstick is negative for protein. Which is the most likely cause of her ankle swelling?
why_correct: Dihydropyridine calcium-channel blockers such as amlodipine dilate precapillary arterioles, raising capillary pressure and causing dependent ankle oedema. It is common, dose-related and occurs without signs of fluid overload. Options include reducing the dose or switching or adding another antihypertensive; diuretics are generally ineffective for this type of oedema.
why_wrong: B. Heart failure would usually cause breathlessness, orthopnoea, a raised JVP or crackles. C. Bilateral DVT is uncommon and would cause calf pain and tenderness rather than symmetrical evening swelling. D. Nephrotic syndrome causes heavy proteinuria, which is absent. E. Hypothyroidism causes non-pitting swelling with other systemic features and is not linked to starting amlodipine.
pearl: Ankle oedema from amlodipine responds poorly to diuretics because it is caused by vasodilation, not fluid retention.
thinking: Bilateral ankle swelling after starting amlodipine ↓ No breathlessness, normal JVP and clear chest ↓ No proteinuria or calf tenderness ↓ Calcium-channel blocker-induced peripheral oedema
exam_trap: B, heart failure — tempting because ankle swelling is a classic sign of it, but she has no breathlessness, a normal JVP and a clear chest.
takeaway: Bilateral ankle oedema without fluid overload soon after starting amlodipine is a drug adverse effect.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15209). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 41-year-old man sees his GP because he has felt on edge and irritable for two months. He has lost weight although he is eating more than usual, his stools have become looser and more frequent, and he sweats and feels uncomfortably warm in an office his colleagues find cold. His pulse is fast and regular, his outstretched hands show a fine tremor, his upper lids lag behind the eyes on looking down, and he has a smooth, non-tender swelling in the front of his neck. What is the likeliest diagnosis?
why_correct: Weight loss with increased appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, frequent stools, tachycardia, fine tremor, lid lag and a diffuse goitre are classic features of thyroid hormone excess. The next step is thyroid function tests, which would show a suppressed TSH with raised free thyroid hormones. Beta-blockers can relieve adrenergic symptoms while the cause is established.
why_wrong: A. Anxiety can cause irritability, sweating and tremor but not weight loss with increased appetite, lid lag or a goitre. B. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic headaches, sweating and palpitations with hypertension rather than a goitre. C. Type 1 diabetes causes weight loss with thirst and polyuria, not heat intolerance or lid lag. E. Hypothyroidism causes weight gain, cold intolerance and bradycardia.
pearl: Always check thyroid function before diagnosing anxiety in someone with weight loss, palpitations and tremor.
thinking: Weight loss despite increased appetite ↓ Heat intolerance, sweating, loose stools ↓ Tachycardia, tremor, lid lag and goitre ↓ Hyperthyroidism
exam_trap: A, generalised anxiety disorder — tempting because irritability, sweating and tremor overlap, but anxiety does not cause weight loss with a big appetite, lid lag or a goitre.
takeaway: Weight loss with a good appetite, heat intolerance, tremor and goitre is hyperthyroidism: check thyroid function.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15114). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Duty of candour after a medication error
stem: While reviewing the drug chart on a medical ward, an FY1 doctor notices that a 74-year-old woman received two doses of enoxaparin overnight instead of one, because the dose had been written up twice. She has no bleeding and her observations are stable. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Take no further action, as no harm has occurred
options.B: Inform the patient only if she later develops bleeding
options.C: Ask the nurse to complete an incident form without discussing it with the patient
options.D: Correct the drug chart quietly so the duplicate entry is no longer visible
options.E: Explain to the patient what happened, apologise, and report it as an incident

correct_answer: E. Explain to the patient what happened, apologise, and report it as an incident
why_correct: GMC guidance on the professional duty of candour requires doctors to be open and honest with patients when something goes wrong with their care that causes, or has the potential to cause, harm or distress. A duplicated anticoagulant dose has that potential even though no harm has yet occurred. She should be told what happened, offered an apology and an explanation of any monitoring needed, and the error should be reported through the local incident system so the cause can be addressed. The doctor should also inform the senior team and ensure she is monitored for bleeding.
why_wrong: A. Candour and incident reporting apply even when no harm results. B. Delaying disclosure until harm occurs is not open or honest. C. Reporting without telling the patient fails the duty to be open with her. D. Altering records to conceal an error is dishonest and a serious probity breach.
pearl: Candour applies to every error that affects a patient, harmful or not: tell the patient, apologise, explain, report, and learn. An apology is not an admission of legal liability.
thinking: Duplicate anticoagulant dose given ↓ No harm so far, but an error has occurred ↓ GMC duty of candour and need for system learning ↓ Tell the patient, apologise, and report it
exam_trap: C, Ask the nurse to complete an incident form without discussing it with the patient — reporting is correct, but leaving the patient uninformed breaches the duty of candour.
takeaway: After any error, be open with the patient, apologise and report it, even if no harm.

stem: A 13-year-old girl attends the emergency department with a sprained wrist. While her arm is being examined, she tells the doctor that her stepfather often hits her with a belt when he has been drinking, and she begs the doctor not to tell anyone because she is frightened of what will happen. How should the doctor respond?

options.A: Keep the information confidential because she is competent to make this decision
options.B: Explain that this cannot be kept secret and follow the hospital's safeguarding procedures
options.C: Speak to the stepfather about the allegation before taking further action
options.D: Discharge her and ask her GP to follow up the concern
options.E: Ask her to write a full statement before deciding whether to act

correct_answer: B. Explain that this cannot be kept secret and follow the hospital's safeguarding procedures
why_correct: A disclosure of physical abuse by a child means she may be at risk of significant harm, which justifies sharing information without consent to protect her. The doctor should listen, avoid making promises of secrecy, explain gently who will need to know and why, document her words accurately, and escalate the same day to the safeguarding lead or children's social care in line with local procedures.
why_wrong: A. Confidentiality can be overridden when a child is at risk of serious harm, even if she is competent. C. Confronting the alleged abuser can increase the danger to the child and compromise any investigation. D. Passing the concern to the GP delays action and may leave her unprotected. E. Asking a child to write a formal statement is inappropriate questioning and delays protection.
pearl: Never promise a child secrecy. Listen, record their words verbatim, explain who needs to know, and escalate to the safeguarding lead or social care the same day.
thinking: Child discloses physical abuse at home ↓ Risk of significant harm overrides confidentiality ↓ Do not promise secrecy or confront the alleged abuser ↓ Follow safeguarding procedures and escalate promptly
exam_trap: A, Keep the information confidential because she is competent — her competence matters for consent to treatment, but a risk of serious harm justifies sharing information to protect her.
takeaway: When a child discloses abuse, never promise secrecy; follow safeguarding procedures.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15077). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Mechanism of iron deficiency in malabsorption
stem: A 33-year-old woman with coeliac disease admits she has not been following her gluten-free diet. She has bloating, pale bulky stools and lost weight. Her periods are light, and she has no gastrointestinal bleeding symptoms. Blood tests show a microcytic anaemia with a low ferritin. How has her anaemia most likely arisen?

options.A: Reduced iron absorption from damaged duodenal mucosa
options.B: Chronic blood loss from intestinal ulceration
options.C: Haemolysis of red cells in the spleen

correct_answer: A. Reduced iron absorption from damaged duodenal mucosa
why_correct: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and upper jejunum, which are the parts of the small bowel most affected by villous atrophy in coeliac disease. Continued gluten exposure therefore impairs iron absorption, leading to iron-deficiency anaemia alongside steatorrhoea and weight loss. Strict adherence to a gluten-free diet allows mucosal healing, with iron replacement as needed.
why_wrong: B. Coeliac disease does not typically cause significant intestinal bleeding, and she has no bleeding symptoms. C. Haemolysis causes a normocytic or macrocytic anaemia with normal or high ferritin. D. Marrow infiltration usually causes pancytopenia rather than isolated iron deficiency. E. Anaemia of chronic inflammation is associated with a normal or raised ferritin.
pearl: Coeliac disease damages the proximal small bowel, where iron and folate are absorbed, so it can cause iron deficiency, folate deficiency or a mixed picture. Unexplained iron deficiency warrants coeliac serology.
thinking: Coeliac disease with ongoing gluten intake ↓ Villous atrophy in the duodenum ↓ Duodenum is the main site of iron absorption ↓ Iron-deficiency anaemia from malabsorption
exam_trap: B, Chronic blood loss from intestinal ulceration — blood loss is the commonest cause of iron deficiency, but in untreated coeliac disease the problem is impaired absorption.
takeaway: In coeliac disease, iron deficiency is due to reduced absorption in the damaged duodenum.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15396). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: During a ward round, a foundation doctor learns that a 63-year-old woman was given a dose of lactulose overnight that had been prescribed for the patient in the neighbouring bed. She is well, her observations are normal and she has come to no harm. How should the doctor respond?

options.A: Take no action because there was no harm
options.B: Explain to the patient what happened and report it through the local incident reporting system
options.C: Report the nurse to the Nursing and Midwifery Council
options.D: Amend the drug chart to show lactulose was prescribed for her
options.E: Inform the patient only if she develops side effects

correct_answer: B. Explain to the patient what happened and report it through the local incident reporting system
why_correct: Errors that reach a patient should be reported through the local incident reporting system even when no harm results, so that contributing factors can be reviewed and learning shared. GMC guidance expects doctors to be open and honest with patients when things go wrong, so she should be told what happened and offered an apology.
why_wrong: A. Lack of harm does not remove the need to report; the same system failure could harm the next patient. C. Referral to a regulator is not an appropriate first response to a single error without evidence of misconduct, and does not address system causes. D. Altering records to conceal an error is dishonest and a serious probity breach. E. Withholding information until harm occurs is incompatible with openness.
pearl: NHS incident reporting focuses on learning from systems rather than blame; no-harm incidents and near misses are valuable sources of that learning.
thinking: Wrong patient received a medicine ↓ error reached the patient but caused no harm ↓ be open with the patient ↓ report locally for learning
exam_trap: A, take no action because there was no harm — tempting because the patient is well, but unreported errors recur; reporting is about preventing future harm.
takeaway: Report every medication error, even without harm, and be open with the patient.

stem: A 72-year-old man is reviewed on a stroke rehabilitation ward three weeks after a left middle cerebral artery infarct. Nursing staff report that he coughs and splutters during meals and his voice sounds wet and gurgly after drinks. He has had two chest infections since admission. Which underlying problem best explains these findings?

options.E: Hospital-acquired infection from poor hand hygiene

correct_answer: A. Aspiration due to unsafe swallowing
why_correct: Coughing while eating and drinking, a wet voice after swallowing and recurrent chest infections indicate dysphagia with aspiration, a common complication after stroke. Oral intake should be reviewed and his swallow formally reassessed by a speech and language therapist, who can advise on safe food and fluid textures and positioning.
why_wrong: B. Reflux causes heartburn and regurgitation, not coughing during swallowing with a wet voice. C. Heart failure causes breathlessness and orthopnoea, not symptoms linked to eating. D. Bronchiectasis causes chronic daily productive cough and would not begin with a stroke. E. Hospital infection does not explain coughing specifically during meals.
pearl: Patients with acute stroke should have their swallow screened before receiving any food, fluid or oral medication, with specialist assessment if the screen is failed.
thinking: Recent stroke ↓ coughing during meals and wet voice after drinks ↓ recurrent chest infections ↓ aspiration from unsafe swallowing
exam_trap: E, hospital-acquired infection from poor hand hygiene — recurrent inpatient chest infections tempt this, but the link to eating and a wet voice points to aspiration.
takeaway: Coughing on eating, a wet voice and recurrent chest infections after stroke mean aspiration: get a swallow assessment.

stem: A 55-year-old woman reports feeling tired and itchy for several months. She does not drink alcohol and has no pain. Her liver function tests show an ALP several times the upper limit of normal, a raised GGT and an ALT that is only slightly elevated. Bilirubin and albumin are normal. Which pattern of liver injury do these results indicate?

options.C: Bone disease such as Paget disease

why_correct: A predominant rise in ALP, confirmed as hepatic in origin by a raised GGT, with only a modest rise in transaminases, indicates a cholestatic pattern. Itch and fatigue in a middle-aged woman with this pattern raise the possibility of primary biliary cholangitis. An ultrasound to exclude duct obstruction and autoantibody testing are appropriate next steps.
why_wrong: A. A hepatocellular pattern shows transaminases rising much more than ALP. C. Bone disease raises ALP but leaves GGT normal. D. Haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin and LDH rather than ALP and GGT. E. Gilbert syndrome causes isolated mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia with otherwise normal liver tests.
pearl: GGT helps localise a raised ALP: a raised GGT suggests a liver source, a normal GGT suggests bone. Itch is a hallmark symptom of cholestasis.
thinking: ALP raised far more than ALT ↓ GGT also raised, so ALP is hepatic ↓ itch and fatigue ↓ cholestatic pattern
exam_trap: C, bone disease such as Paget disease — a raised ALP in middle age tempts this, but bone disease does not raise GGT.
takeaway: Raised ALP with raised GGT and only a modest transaminase rise indicates a cholestatic pattern.

stem: A 58-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by ambulance. Her husband found her at breakfast with a drooping face, slurred speech and a weak right arm; she had been seen well less than an hour earlier. Her capillary glucose is normal and she is haemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.B: Arrange an immediate non-contrast CT head as part of urgent stroke team assessment
options.D: Admit to a general medical ward for observation
options.E: Request an MRI head within the next 24 hours

correct_answer: B. Arrange an immediate non-contrast CT head as part of urgent stroke team assessment
why_correct: Sudden facial weakness, dysarthria and arm weakness with a recent known onset is an acute stroke until proven otherwise. She needs immediate assessment by the stroke team and urgent brain imaging, usually non-contrast CT, to exclude haemorrhage and decide on thrombolysis or thrombectomy. These treatments are time-critical, so imaging must not be delayed.
why_wrong: A. Aspirin must not be given until haemorrhage has been excluded by imaging. C. Carotid imaging is part of later work-up for anterior circulation events, not the immediate priority. D. Observation on a general ward delays time-critical treatment. E. Waiting for MRI would miss the window for reperfusion treatment.
pearl: Check glucose early in suspected stroke, as hypoglycaemia can mimic it; then image immediately, because every minute of delay to reperfusion costs brain tissue.
thinking: Sudden unilateral face and arm weakness with dysarthria ↓ recent known onset, glucose normal ↓ must exclude haemorrhage before reperfusion ↓ immediate stroke assessment and CT head
exam_trap: A, give aspirin straight away — antiplatelet therapy is part of ischaemic stroke care, but giving it before imaging risks worsening an intracerebral haemorrhage.
takeaway: Suspected acute stroke needs immediate stroke team assessment and brain imaging before any antithrombotic.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of another item in same pack). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 34-year-old man attends the emergency department with a week of tiredness, breathlessness on climbing stairs and dark urine. His sclerae are yellow and the spleen tip is just palpable. Investigations reveal a low haemoglobin with a normal mean cell volume, an elevated reticulocyte count, a raised unconjugated bilirubin and a raised lactate dehydrogenase. Liver enzymes are normal. Which process best explains his anaemia?

options.A: Impaired DNA synthesis in red-cell precursors

why_correct: A raised reticulocyte count shows that the marrow is responding vigorously, while raised unconjugated bilirubin and lactate dehydrogenase reflect red cells being broken down. Together with jaundice, dark urine and splenomegaly, this indicates haemolysis, and a direct antiglobulin test and blood film are the next useful investigations.
why_wrong: A. Impaired DNA synthesis from B12 or folate deficiency causes a macrocytic anaemia with a low reticulocyte count. B. Reduced erythropoietin, as in chronic kidney disease, gives a normocytic anaemia with a poor reticulocyte response. D. Marrow infiltration suppresses production, so the reticulocyte count is low and the film may be leucoerythroblastic. E. Iron-restricted production causes a microcytic anaemia without reticulocytosis or jaundice.
pearl: Separate anaemias by the reticulocyte count: high means loss or destruction, low means underproduction. Add raised unconjugated bilirubin and LDH and you have haemolysis.
thinking: Normocytic anaemia ↓ reticulocytes raised, so marrow is working hard ↓ raised unconjugated bilirubin and LDH with jaundice and dark urine ↓ Increased red-cell destruction
exam_trap: B, Reduced erythropoietin production — a normocytic anaemia often points to chronic disease or renal causes, but these underproduction states have a low reticulocyte count and no jaundice.
takeaway: Normocytic anaemia with reticulocytosis and raised unconjugated bilirubin means haemolysis.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15173). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 39-year-old woman is on the surgical ward the day after a total thyroidectomy. She complains of numbness around her lips and pins and needles in her fingers. Her adjusted calcium is low. Which neuromuscular finding is most likely to be present?

options.E: Ptosis that worsens through the day

why_correct: Low calcium lowers the threshold for nerve firing, causing perioral and peripheral paraesthesia, muscle cramps and tetany such as carpopedal spasm, which can be provoked by inflating a blood pressure cuff (Trousseau sign). After thyroidectomy this usually reflects parathyroid damage, and symptomatic patients need calcium replacement with ECG monitoring.
why_wrong: A. Intention tremor indicates cerebellar disease. B. Flaccid areflexic weakness is more typical of severe hypokalaemia or Guillain–Barré syndrome, not the hyperexcitability of low calcium. D. Tongue fasciculations suggest motor neurone disease. E. Fatigable ptosis is a feature of myasthenia gravis.
pearl: Low calcium makes nerves irritable: perioral tingling, cramps, carpopedal spasm and Chvostek and Trousseau signs. Watch for laryngospasm, seizures and a prolonged QT interval.
thinking: Day one after total thyroidectomy ↓ perioral and finger paraesthesia with low calcium ↓ hypocalcaemia increases neuromuscular excitability ↓ Carpopedal spasm
exam_trap: B, Flaccid weakness with absent reflexes — electrolyte disturbances commonly cause weakness, but low calcium causes hyperexcitability and spasm rather than flaccid paralysis.
takeaway: Hypocalcaemia causes perioral tingling and carpopedal spasm from neuromuscular hyperexcitability.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ16261). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Helicobacter pylori and peptic ulcer disease
stem: A 39-year-old woman tells her GP she has had a gnawing pain in her upper abdomen for two months. It often wakes her in the early hours and eases when she eats or drinks milk. She has no weight loss, vomiting or anaemia. A stool antigen test is positive for Helicobacter pylori. Which condition is this infection most likely to have caused?
why_correct: H. pylori causes chronic gastritis, increases acid output and damages the mucosal defence, making it a leading cause of peptic ulceration, particularly duodenal ulcers. Night-time epigastric pain that eases with food is typical of a duodenal ulcer. Eradication therapy with a proton pump inhibitor and two antibiotics heals ulcers and reduces recurrence.
why_wrong: A. Barrett oesophagus results from long-standing acid reflux, not H. pylori. C. Eosinophilic oesophagitis is allergic, causing dysphagia and food bolus impaction. D. Coeliac disease is immune-mediated gluten sensitivity unrelated to H. pylori. E. Gallstones cause postprandial right upper quadrant pain and are not linked to H. pylori.
pearl: Before H. pylori testing, stop proton pump inhibitors for two weeks and antibiotics for four weeks to avoid false negatives. H. pylori is also linked to gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma.
thinking: Epigastric pain waking her at night ↓ eased by food ↓ no alarm features ↓ positive H. pylori stool antigen ↓ duodenal ulcer
exam_trap: A, Barrett oesophagus — it is linked with upper GI symptoms and cancer risk, but it arises from reflux, not H. pylori infection.
takeaway: H. pylori is a major cause of peptic ulcer disease, especially duodenal ulcers.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15249). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: An 18-month-old boy who has just started walking is brought to the emergency department with a hot, swollen, painful right knee after a minor fall. His mother says he bruises easily, and her brother had a bleeding problem needing regular injections. Platelet count and prothrombin time are normal, but the APTT is longer than the reference range. Which inherited condition best explains these findings?
why_correct: Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) and B (factor IX deficiency) are X-linked, so they affect boys and pass through carrier mothers to their sons, such as a maternal uncle. Deficiency of these intrinsic pathway factors prolongs the APTT with a normal PT and platelet count. Deep tissue and joint bleeding (haemarthrosis), often appearing as a child starts to walk, is typical.
why_wrong: A. Von Willebrand disease is autosomal and usually causes mucocutaneous bleeding such as nosebleeds and gum bleeding rather than haemarthrosis. C. Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia causes nosebleeds and telangiectasia with normal clotting tests. D. Sickle cell disease causes painful crises and haemolysis, not a prolonged APTT. E. Hereditary spherocytosis causes haemolysis and jaundice, not bleeding.
pearl: In any child with unexplained bruising, check clotting and the family history, but also remember safeguarding; a bleeding disorder and non-accidental injury can coexist.
thinking: Boy with haemarthrosis after minor trauma ↓ affected maternal uncle = X-linked pattern ↓ normal platelets and PT ↓ prolonged APTT = intrinsic factor deficiency ↓ haemophilia
exam_trap: A, von Willebrand disease — it is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder and can prolong the APTT, but it is autosomal and joint bleeds are unusual.
takeaway: Haemarthrosis in a boy with an isolated prolonged APTT and an affected maternal uncle suggests haemophilia.

stem: A 72-year-old man with lung cancer receiving palliative care is visited at home by his GP. Over three days he has become unsteady and both legs feel numb from his navel downwards. He has a mid-back pain that is worse when he coughs. He has not passed urine since the morning and a tender, distended bladder is palpable. He is fully orientated. Which diagnosis must be considered urgently?
why_correct: Back pain worse on coughing with progressive leg symptoms, a sensory level on the trunk and urinary retention in a patient with cancer are features of spinal cord compression. Lung cancer frequently spreads to the spine. Even in palliative care, prompt recognition matters because urgent treatment can preserve mobility and continence and improve quality of life.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia causes confusion, thirst, constipation and fatigue, not a sensory level. C. Brain metastases cause headache, seizures or focal weakness, not a sensory level with retention in an orientated patient. D. Peripheral neuropathy causes glove-and-stocking sensory loss, not a truncal level or retention. E. Opioids can cause retention but do not explain leg numbness with a sensory level.
pearl: A sensory level on the trunk localises the problem to the spinal cord. A level at the umbilicus corresponds to the T10 dermatome, and because cord segments lie higher than their matching vertebrae, the compressing lesion is at or above that level and often at a higher vertebral level than expected.
thinking: Known lung cancer ↓ mid-back pain worse on coughing ↓ leg numbness with a truncal sensory level ↓ urinary retention ↓ metastatic spinal cord compression
exam_trap: E, opioid-induced urinary retention — palliative patients on opioids often retain urine, but this does not explain the sensory level and unsteadiness.
takeaway: A sensory level with leg weakness and retention in cancer means spinal cord compression.

stem: A 19-month-old girl whose parents declined MMR vaccination is brought to the GP. She has had a low-grade temperature and a faint pink rash that started on her face and spread to her trunk over a day. She is otherwise playful. There are tender enlarged lymph nodes behind her ears and at the back of her neck. Her aunt, who looks after her daily, is 9 weeks pregnant and unsure of her own vaccination history. Which infection is most likely, and of most concern for the aunt's pregnancy?
why_correct: A mild illness with a pink maculopapular rash spreading from the face downwards and postauricular and suboccipital lymphadenopathy in an unvaccinated child suggests rubella. Infection in early pregnancy carries a high risk of congenital rubella syndrome, including deafness, cataracts and heart defects. Rubella is notifiable, and the pregnant contact needs urgent assessment and serology.
why_wrong: A. Roseola causes high fever for several days followed by a rash as the fever settles, and carries no recognised fetal risk. B. Scarlet fever causes a sandpaper rash with sore throat and strawberry tongue. D. Hand, foot and mouth disease causes mouth ulcers and vesicles on the hands and feet. E. Erythema infectiosum (parvovirus B19) causes slapped cheeks followed by a lacy rash on the limbs, and its fetal risk is anaemia and hydrops rather than malformations.
pearl: Any pregnant woman exposed to a rash illness should have her immune status checked urgently, as management depends on the likely infection and her stage of pregnancy.
thinking: Unvaccinated child ↓ mild fever, pink rash spreading from face downwards ↓ postauricular and suboccipital nodes ↓ pregnant contact at risk of congenital infection ↓ rubella
exam_trap: E, erythema infectiosum — parvovirus also endangers a pregnancy, but it gives slapped cheeks and a lacy limb rash, and its risk is fetal anaemia rather than malformation.
takeaway: Rash with postauricular nodes in an unvaccinated child suggests rubella; urgently assess any pregnant contact.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15263). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 44-year-old woman was diagnosed with high blood pressure at the age of 40. Despite taking three antihypertensive drugs, none of them a diuretic, her home readings remain high. Repeated blood tests show a low serum potassium with normal renal function. She mentions muscle weakness and getting up at night to pass urine. She has no Cushingoid features and no episodes of palpitations or sweating. Which underlying cause is most likely?
why_correct: Hypertension that is difficult to control together with unexplained low potassium, particularly when not on a diuretic, should prompt screening for primary hyperaldosteronism. Autonomous aldosterone production from an adrenal adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia causes sodium retention and potassium loss. The first test is an aldosterone-to-renin ratio, which would show high aldosterone with suppressed renin.
why_wrong: B. Phaeochromocytoma causes episodic headache, palpitations and sweating rather than persistent hypokalaemia. C. Cushing's syndrome can cause hypertension and low potassium but would usually show central obesity, striae or bruising. D. Renal artery stenosis can raise blood pressure but usually affects renal function, especially after starting an ACE inhibitor. E. Addison's disease causes low blood pressure and high potassium, the opposite picture.
pearl: Think of primary hyperaldosteronism in young or resistant hypertension, or hypertension with low potassium. Screen with an aldosterone-to-renin ratio, ideally with potassium corrected first.
thinking: Early-onset hypertension ↓ Resistant to three drugs ↓ Low potassium without a diuretic ↓ Weakness and nocturia from hypokalaemia ↓ Primary hyperaldosteronism
exam_trap: D, renal artery stenosis — it is a classic secondary cause of resistant hypertension and can also lower potassium, but normal renal function and no other vascular clues make primary aldosterone excess more likely.
takeaway: Resistant hypertension with unexplained low potassium: screen for primary hyperaldosteronism.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15778). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: An 81-year-old man is brought to his GP by his daughter. Over the past two years he has repeatedly asked the same questions, has got lost driving to familiar places and has forgotten to pay bills. He is alert during the consultation and his performance has not changed from day to day. He sleeps well and says his mood is good. Blood tests are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: A gradual, progressive decline in memory and other cognitive abilities over years, severe enough to affect daily activities such as driving and managing money, is dementia. His normal alertness and stable performance distinguish it from delirium. He should have a structured cognitive assessment and be referred to a memory service.
why_wrong: A. Delirium has an acute onset with fluctuating attention and conscious level. C. Depression can cause poor concentration, but his mood and sleep are normal. D. Normal ageing may slow recall but does not stop someone from managing familiar tasks such as finances or driving. E. Late-onset schizophrenia presents with delusions and hallucinations rather than progressive memory loss.
pearl: Key questions in cognitive impairment are timeline and attention: years with clear attention suggests dementia; hours to days with fluctuating attention suggests delirium.
thinking: Gradual decline over two years ↓ Memory and orientation problems ↓ Impact on daily function ↓ Alert with stable attention ↓ Dementia
exam_trap: A, delirium — confusion in an older person often prompts it, but delirium is acute and fluctuating, while this is slow and steady.
takeaway: Slow progressive cognitive decline affecting daily life, with clear attention, is dementia.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ11981). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 35-year-old woman with Crohn's disease has needed high-dose prednisolone for most of the past six months because of repeated flares. At clinic she says her face has become rounder, she has wide purple stretch marks on her abdomen, a fatty hump has appeared between her shoulders and she bruises easily. Her blood pressure and blood glucose have risen. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Cushing's disease from a pituitary adenoma

why_correct: Prolonged high-dose glucocorticoid treatment is by far the commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome. Moon face, purple striae, a dorsocervical fat pad, easy bruising, hypertension and hyperglycaemia are classic features of glucocorticoid excess. Management involves using the lowest effective steroid dose and steroid-sparing treatment for her Crohn's disease, without stopping prednisolone abruptly.
why_wrong: A. Cushing's disease is a rare endogenous cause and is unlikely when there is clear exposure to high-dose steroids. B. Hypothyroidism causes weight gain and fatigue but not striae, bruising or a dorsocervical fat pad. D. PCOS causes weight gain and hirsutism but not striae with bruising and hypertension. E. Adrenal insufficiency causes weight loss and low blood pressure, the opposite picture.
pearl: Always ask about steroid use, including inhaled, topical and injected forms, before investigating for endogenous Cushing's syndrome.
thinking: Months of high-dose prednisolone ↓ Moon face, striae, buffalo hump ↓ Easy bruising ↓ Hypertension and hyperglycaemia ↓ Iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome
exam_trap: A, Cushing's disease — the clinical features are identical, but exogenous steroid exposure is far commoner and explains the picture without a pituitary tumour.
takeaway: Cushingoid features in someone on long-term steroids are iatrogenic until proven otherwise.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15999). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: At her booking appointment, a 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy is found to be blood group O RhD-negative with no red cell antibodies. Her partner is RhD-positive. The midwife explains that she will be offered routine anti-D immunoglobulin in the third trimester. What is the main purpose of this treatment?

options.B: To prevent maternal sensitisation to fetal RhD antigen
options.C: To prevent ABO incompatibility in the newborn
options.D: To reduce the risk of pre-eclampsia
options.E: To neutralise anti-D antibodies she already has

correct_answer: B. To prevent maternal sensitisation to fetal RhD antigen
why_correct: If an RhD-negative woman is exposed to RhD-positive fetal red cells, she may produce anti-D antibodies that cross the placenta and cause haemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, mainly in later pregnancies. Anti-D immunoglobulin clears fetal red cells from her circulation before her immune system responds. Routine antenatal prophylaxis, together with doses after sensitising events and after birth if the baby is RhD-positive, greatly reduces this risk.
why_wrong: A. Anti-D is preventive and does not treat fetal anaemia, which needs specialist fetal medicine care. C. Anti-D has no effect on ABO incompatibility. D. Anti-D does not affect the risk of pre-eclampsia. E. Anti-D cannot reverse sensitisation once a woman has formed her own antibodies.
pearl: Give anti-D after potentially sensitising events such as abdominal trauma, bleeding after 12 weeks, external cephalic version and amniocentesis, in addition to routine prophylaxis.
thinking: RhD-negative mother, RhD-positive partner ↓ Fetus may be RhD-positive ↓ Fetal cells entering maternal circulation ↓ Anti-D clears them before an immune response ↓ Prevents maternal sensitisation
exam_trap: A, treat existing fetal anaemia — anti-D is associated with haemolytic disease, but it is prophylactic and only works before the mother has been sensitised.
takeaway: Anti-D prevents RhD-negative mothers from becoming sensitised to fetal RhD-positive cells.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15236). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to the GP because several children at her nursery have been unwell. She has had a mild fever for two days and very itchy spots that started on her scalp and chest. On examination there are red papules, clear fluid-filled blisters and crusted lesions side by side, mostly on the trunk, with a few shallow ulcers inside her mouth. Her palms and soles are spared. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Chickenpox causes intensely itchy crops of lesions that progress from papules to vesicles to crusts, so lesions at different stages are seen together. The rash is concentrated on the trunk, scalp and face and may involve the mouth. Management is usually supportive, with advice on keeping her away from nursery until all lesions have crusted.
why_wrong: A. Hand, foot and mouth disease causes mouth ulcers with vesicles on the hands and feet, which are spared here. B. Measles causes a maculopapular rash that starts behind the ears, with cough, conjunctivitis and coryza. C. Impetigo causes honey-crusted lesions, usually around the nose and mouth, not widespread vesicles. E. Scarlet fever causes a fine sandpaper-like rash with a strawberry tongue and sore throat.
pearl: Lesions at different stages concentrated on the trunk point to chickenpox. Avoid NSAIDs in chickenpox because of the association with severe skin infection.
thinking: Nursery outbreak, mild fever ↓ Very itchy rash starting on scalp and chest ↓ Papules, vesicles and crusts together ↓ Truncal distribution, palms spared ↓ Chickenpox
exam_trap: A, hand, foot and mouth disease — mouth ulcers with vesicles in a nursery child suggest it, but the truncal rash with crops at different stages and spared palms and soles fit chickenpox.
takeaway: Itchy truncal crops of papules, vesicles and crusts together indicate chickenpox.

stem: A 24-year-old woman attends a sexual health clinic because she has noticed several soft lumps around her vulva and perianal skin over the past two months. Some are single and some form clusters. Examination shows skin-coloured, raised lesions with an irregular, warty surface. They are not tender and none have a central dimple. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Painless, skin-coloured, raised lesions with a rough cauliflower-like surface around the genitals and perianal area are anogenital warts. They are caused by human papillomavirus, usually types 6 and 11. Treatment options include topical agents such as podophyllotoxin or imiquimod, or cryotherapy, and a full sexual health screen should be offered.
why_wrong: A. Molluscum lesions are smooth, pearly papules with a central dimple. C. Condylomata lata are flat, moist, greyish plaques of secondary syphilis rather than cauliflower-like papules. D. Lichen sclerosus causes white, thin, itchy patches rather than raised warty lumps. E. Herpes causes painful blisters and ulcers.
pearl: HPV vaccination protects against both genital warts and cervical cancer-causing types. Warts are often multiple and may recur after treatment.
thinking: Painless raised genital lumps ↓ Skin-coloured and warty surface ↓ Clusters on vulva and perianal skin ↓ No central dimple, no ulceration ↓ Anogenital warts
exam_trap: A, molluscum contagiosum — it also causes painless genital papules in young adults, but they are smooth and dimpled rather than rough and warty.
takeaway: Painless cauliflower-like genital lumps are anogenital warts caused by HPV.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ14796). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 28-year-old woman sees her GP with two months of loose stools several times a day and crampy lower abdominal pain. There has been no foreign travel and stool cultures are negative. Her coeliac serology is negative, and her faecal calprotectin comes back markedly raised. How should this result be interpreted?
correct_answer: B. Inflammation of the intestinal mucosa
why_correct: Calprotectin is a protein released by neutrophils, so its level in stool rises when there is inflammation of the bowel wall. A markedly raised result in a young adult with chronic diarrhoea suggests inflammatory bowel disease rather than a functional disorder. She should be referred for specialist assessment and colonoscopy.
why_wrong: A. IBS does not cause intestinal inflammation, so calprotectin is typically normal. C. Calprotectin does not diagnose coeliac disease, which is assessed by serology and duodenal biopsy. D. Pancreatic insufficiency is assessed with faecal elastase, not calprotectin. E. A raised calprotectin is not specific for cancer and cannot confirm it.
pearl: Faecal calprotectin helps distinguish IBD from IBS in younger adults with lower gastrointestinal symptoms; it is not a cancer test and can also be raised by infection or NSAIDs.
thinking: Chronic diarrhoea and cramps ↓ Infection and coeliac disease excluded ↓ Calprotectin comes from neutrophils ↓ Markedly raised result ↓ Inflammation of the intestinal mucosa
exam_trap: D, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency — candidates confuse the two stool tests, but pancreatic function is assessed by faecal elastase, while calprotectin reflects gut inflammation.
takeaway: Raised faecal calprotectin indicates intestinal inflammation, favouring IBD over IBS.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15875). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 74-year-old man attends his GP because his wife noticed his eyes have turned yellow. He has lost weight over two months and has generalised itching. He says his urine looks like strong tea and his stools are pale grey. He has no abdominal pain, and examination reveals a smooth, non-tender mass below the right costal margin. Which bilirubin pattern would you expect?
why_correct: Painless jaundice with pale stools, dark urine, pruritus, weight loss and a palpable gallbladder suggests obstruction of the common bile duct, for example by pancreatic cancer. Bilirubin that has been conjugated in the liver cannot drain into the gut, so stool loses its colour, while water-soluble conjugated bilirubin passes into the urine. He needs urgent investigation on a suspected cancer pathway.
why_wrong: B. Unconjugated bilirubin is not water-soluble, so it does not darken urine, and stools remain normal. C. Jaundice means bilirubin is raised, so it cannot be normal. D. Bilirubin cannot be low in a jaundiced patient, and reticulocytes relate to haemolysis. E. Haemolysis causes unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia without pale stools or dark urine.
pearl: A palpable, non-tender gallbladder with painless jaundice suggests malignant obstruction rather than gallstones (Courvoisier's law).
thinking: Painless jaundice with weight loss ↓ Dark urine and pale stools ↓ Pruritus from bile salts ↓ Palpable gallbladder from distal obstruction ↓ Conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia
exam_trap: B, unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia — candidates mix up the types, but only conjugated bilirubin is water-soluble enough to darken urine, and pale stools show bile is not reaching the gut.
takeaway: Jaundice with dark urine and pale stools indicates conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia from obstruction.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15873). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 59-year-old man with alcohol-related liver disease sees his GP because his trousers no longer fasten and his ankles are swollen. His abdomen is distended with bulging flanks. Percussion is resonant centrally and dull in the flanks, and when he rolls onto his right side the area of dullness moves. What best explains the distension?
why_correct: Dullness in the flanks that moves to the dependent side on turning (shifting dullness) indicates free fluid in the peritoneal cavity. Ascites is a common sign of decompensated cirrhosis, caused by portal hypertension, low albumin and sodium retention. He needs a diagnostic ascitic tap to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, salt restriction and usually spironolactone.
why_wrong: A. Gaseous distension gives resonance throughout and no shifting dullness. C. Hepatomegaly causes a palpable liver edge in the right upper quadrant rather than shifting flank dullness. D. Urinary retention causes a suprapubic mass that is dull centrally, not in the flanks. E. Obesity causes generalised distension without shifting dullness.
pearl: New or worsening ascites in cirrhosis should prompt a diagnostic paracentesis to look for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, even without fever or pain.
thinking: Alcohol-related liver disease ↓ Distended abdomen with bulging flanks ↓ Central resonance, flank dullness ↓ Dullness shifts on turning ↓ Ascites
exam_trap: A, gaseous bowel distension — a swollen abdomen may suggest gas or obstruction, but flank dullness that moves with position means free fluid.
takeaway: Shifting dullness in a patient with cirrhosis indicates ascites.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15533). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 52-year-old man sees his GP about a red mark on his thigh. Two weeks ago he removed a small tick from that spot after a walking holiday in the Scottish Highlands. The mark started as a small red spot and has spread outwards over several days to form a large flat ring with a paler centre. It is not scaly, hot or very tender. He feels slightly tired but otherwise well. What is the most likely diagnosis?
correct_answer: D. Erythema migrans of Lyme disease
why_correct: An expanding red ring with central clearing appearing days to weeks after a tick bite is erythema migrans, the hallmark of early Lyme disease caused by Borrelia burgdorferi. NICE advises diagnosing and treating it clinically without blood tests, as serology is often negative early. First-line treatment is a course of oral doxycycline.
why_wrong: A. Tinea corporis forms a ring but has a scaly advancing edge and spreads slowly over weeks. B. Cellulitis is hot, tender and poorly demarcated, without central clearing. C. Granuloma annulare forms rings of skin-coloured papules with no link to a tick bite. E. A fixed drug eruption follows a drug, recurs at the same site and is usually dusky or violaceous.
pearl: Many people with Lyme disease never notice the bite. Ask about outdoor activity in tick areas, and remember later features such as facial nerve palsy, arthritis and heart block.
thinking: Recent tick exposure in UK countryside ↓ Red lesion expanding from the bite site ↓ Ring with central clearing, not scaly ↓ Clinical diagnosis without serology ↓ Erythema migrans of Lyme disease
exam_trap: A, Tinea corporis — the ring shape is similar, but fungal lesions are scaly and slow-growing, while a non-scaly expanding ring after a tick bite is erythema migrans.
takeaway: An expanding ring after a tick bite is erythema migrans: diagnose clinically and treat with doxycycline.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15740). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 17-year-old girl attends her GP with a widespread itchy, red, blotchy rash that started two days after beginning amoxicillin for a sore throat. She has felt exhausted for a week. Examination shows enlarged, exudative tonsils, petechiae on the soft palate, tender posterior cervical lymph nodes and a palpable spleen tip. Which infection most likely underlies this presentation?
why_correct: Infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein–Barr virus presents with sore throat, fatigue, posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, palatal petechiae and splenomegaly. A large proportion of patients given amoxicillin or ampicillin develop a widespread maculopapular rash, which does not usually indicate true penicillin allergy. A monospot test or EBV serology confirms the diagnosis, and she should avoid contact sports for several weeks because of the risk of splenic rupture.
why_wrong: A. Streptococcal pharyngitis can cause a sandpaper-like scarlatiniform rash, but not splenomegaly, prolonged exhaustion or a rash provoked by amoxicillin. B. Primary HIV can cause fever, sore throat, rash and lymphadenopathy, but the rash is not triggered by amoxicillin and splenomegaly with palatal petechiae favours glandular fever. D. Toxoplasmosis causes lymphadenopathy and mild illness, usually without exudative tonsillitis. E. Measles has a prodrome of cough, coryza and conjunctivitis with a rash spreading from behind the ears.
pearl: Document the amoxicillin rash in glandular fever accurately; wrongly labelling the patient penicillin-allergic for life can restrict future antibiotic choices.
thinking: Teenager with sore throat and marked fatigue ↓ Posterior nodes, palatal petechiae and splenomegaly ↓ Widespread rash after amoxicillin ↓ Classic aminopenicillin reaction in EBV infection ↓ Infectious mononucleosis
exam_trap: A, Group A streptococcal pharyngitis — exudative tonsils and a rash suggest scarlet fever, but splenomegaly, posterior nodes and a rash triggered by amoxicillin point to EBV.
takeaway: Sore throat, splenomegaly and a rash after amoxicillin suggest glandular fever.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ15504). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Valid Advance Decision to Refuse Treatment
stem: A 74-year-old man with motor neurone disease is admitted unconscious with aspiration pneumonia and worsening respiratory failure. A year ago, while he had capacity, he signed a witnessed written advance decision stating that he refuses invasive ventilation even if his life is at risk. The document clearly covers this situation and there is no evidence that he changed his mind. His son asks the team to ventilate him anyway. What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Ventilate him because his son is next of kin and can override the document
options.B: Apply to the Court of Protection before making any decision
options.C: Ventilate temporarily until he regains capacity and can be asked again
options.D: Treat the document as a DNACPR order only and proceed with ventilation
options.E: Respect the advance decision and do not start ventilation, while continuing other care and comfort measures

correct_answer: E. Respect the advance decision and do not start ventilation, while continuing other care and comfort measures
why_correct: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, a valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment has the same force as a refusal made at the time by a patient with capacity. For life-sustaining treatment it must be written, signed, witnessed and state that it applies even if life is at risk, which this does. Clinicians must respect it while continuing other treatment and symptom control, and should explain this sensitively to the family.
why_wrong: A. Relatives cannot override a valid advance decision; next of kin has no legal power to consent on an adult's behalf. B. Court involvement is only needed if there is genuine doubt about validity or applicability, which there is not here. C. Ventilating him would give exactly the treatment he has validly refused. D. The document specifically refuses ventilation and cannot be reinterpreted as a DNACPR order.
pearl: An advance decision can only refuse treatment; it cannot demand specific treatments, and it does not prevent basic comfort care such as warmth, hygiene and offering food and drink by mouth.
thinking: Patient now lacks capacity ↓ Written, signed, witnessed advance refusal of ventilation ↓ States it applies even if life is at risk and covers this situation ↓ Valid and applicable, so legally binding ↓ Respect it and continue other care
exam_trap: B, Applying to the Court of Protection — it seems a cautious safeguard, but it is only needed when validity or applicability is genuinely in doubt, and the delay here would lead to unwanted treatment.
takeaway: A valid, applicable advance refusal of treatment must be respected, even against the family's wishes.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ1099). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: During a GP home visit, a 58-year-old woman treated for breast cancer three years ago describes a band of pain around her chest that has kept her awake for two weeks. Since yesterday she has stumbled several times and says her legs feel numb. Which diagnosis is most important to exclude urgently?
why_correct: Breast cancer commonly spreads to the spine, and band-like thoracic pain with night pain followed by leg numbness and unsteadiness strongly suggests metastatic spinal cord compression, even years after treatment. She needs immediate referral for an MRI of the whole spine and specialist management, because outcome depends on her ability to walk when treatment starts.
why_wrong: A. Hypercalcaemia causes confusion, thirst, constipation and abdominal pain, not a sensory level with leg numbness. B. Guillain-Barré syndrome causes ascending weakness, usually after an infection, without band-like spinal pain. C. Lumbar stenosis causes leg pain on walking eased by bending forward, not band-like thoracic pain with acute numbness. D. Shingles can cause band-like pain but not leg numbness and stumbling.
pearl: Band-like (radicular) pain around the chest or abdomen in a patient with cancer can be an early sign of spinal metastases before any weakness.
thinking: Previous breast cancer ↓ Band-like thoracic pain, worse at night ↓ New leg numbness and stumbling ↓ Spinal metastasis compressing the cord ↓ Exclude metastatic spinal cord compression urgently
exam_trap: D, Shingles affecting a thoracic dermatome — band-like pain fits shingles, which tempts, but it does not explain new leg numbness and falls.
takeaway: Cancer history plus band-like spinal pain and new leg symptoms needs urgent investigation for metastatic spinal cord compression.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN8380). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: Paramedics are called to a house party where a 17-year-old with type 1 diabetes cannot be woken. Friends say he injected his usual insulin, drank alcohol and has not eaten. He is breathing, has a pulse and his capillary glucose meter reads well below normal. Which treatment is appropriate?

options.A: Give an additional dose of long-acting insulin
options.B: Pour a sugary drink into his mouth
options.C: Place him in the recovery position and let him sleep it off
options.D: Give glucose immediately by a parenteral route, such as IV glucose or IM glucagon
options.E: Restrict his carbohydrate intake for the next 24 hours

correct_answer: D. Give glucose immediately by a parenteral route, such as IV glucose or IM glucagon
why_correct: He has severe hypoglycaemia with impaired consciousness, which is an emergency. Because he cannot swallow safely, glucose must be given without relying on the oral route: IV glucose (typically 10%) if access is available, or IM glucagon if not. Once he is awake he needs oral carbohydrate to prevent recurrence.
why_wrong: A. More insulin would deepen the hypoglycaemia. B. Fluids by mouth in an unconscious patient risk aspiration. C. Leaving him to sleep allows ongoing neuroglycopenia and risks brain injury. E. Restricting carbohydrate is the opposite of what he needs.
pearl: Alcohol suppresses hepatic glucose production, so glucagon may be less effective after heavy drinking and IV glucose is preferred where possible.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes, insulin plus alcohol, no food ↓ Unrousable ↓ Very low capillary glucose ↓ Cannot swallow safely ↓ Parenteral glucose or IM glucagon now
exam_trap: B, Sugary drink — oral glucose is the right treatment for a conscious patient, but in someone who cannot be woken it risks aspiration.
takeaway: Severe hypoglycaemia with reduced consciousness needs immediate IV glucose or IM glucagon, not oral treatment.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN10321). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 63-year-old man with lymphoma had his last cycle of chemotherapy eight days ago. He rings the acute oncology helpline because he feels hot and shivery, and his wife has measured a fever. He is asked to attend, and his blood count shows a severely low neutrophil count. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Wait for blood culture results before deciding on antibiotics
options.B: Reassure him that fever is common after chemotherapy
options.C: Treat this as an emergency with urgent assessment and intravenous antibiotics
options.D: Give paracetamol and review him in clinic in two days
options.E: Start G-CSF alone and recheck his blood count

correct_answer: C. Treat this as an emergency with urgent assessment and intravenous antibiotics
why_correct: Fever around a week after chemotherapy with severe neutropenia is neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise. Infection can progress rapidly without the usual signs because there are few neutrophils to mount a response. NICE advises treating suspected neutropenic sepsis as an acute medical emergency and starting empirical intravenous antibiotics immediately.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for cultures delays life-saving treatment. B. Fever with neutropenia must never be dismissed as an expected effect. D. Paracetamol may mask fever and delay treatment. E. G-CSF is not a substitute for antibiotics.
pearl: The neutrophil nadir after most chemotherapy regimens occurs around 7 to 14 days after treatment.
thinking: Recent chemotherapy ↓ Fever and shivering ↓ Severe neutropenia ↓ Neutropenic sepsis until proven otherwise ↓ Urgent assessment and IV antibiotics
exam_trap: E, G-CSF alone — growth factors can shorten neutropenia, which makes this seem logical, but they do not treat the infection.
takeaway: Fever after chemotherapy with neutropenia is an emergency needing immediate intravenous antibiotics.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN3941). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 37-year-old man having chemotherapy for testicular cancer arrives at the acute oncology unit with a fever. A rapid blood count shows severe neutropenia, and blood cultures have already been taken. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.A: G-CSF alone with review in 24 hours
options.B: Empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately, within the first hour
options.C: Wait for blood culture results before starting antibiotics
options.D: Oral antibiotics and a haematology review the next day

correct_answer: B. Empirical broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics immediately, within the first hour
why_correct: Suspected neutropenic sepsis is an acute medical emergency. NICE advises giving empirical intravenous antibiotics immediately, and within an hour of arrival for anyone at high risk of sepsis; with cultures already taken there is no reason to delay. Local protocols usually recommend piperacillin with tazobactam.
why_wrong: A. G-CSF does not treat infection and is not a substitute for antibiotics. C. Waiting for cultures delays urgent treatment. D. Oral therapy with next-day review is unsafe at presentation. E. Platelets and paracetamol do not treat infection.
pearl: Do not wait for the neutrophil count if neutropenic sepsis is suspected clinically; start antibiotics on suspicion.
thinking: Chemotherapy, now febrile ↓ Severe neutropenia ↓ Cultures already taken ↓ Neutropenic sepsis is an emergency ↓ Immediate empirical IV antibiotics
exam_trap: C, Wait for culture results — targeting therapy seems sensible, but untreated neutropenic sepsis can be fatal within hours, so antibiotics come first.
takeaway: In suspected neutropenic sepsis, start empirical intravenous antibiotics immediately.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN3941). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Suspected meningococcal disease in primary care
stem: An out-of-hours GP visits a 7-year-old boy at home. His mother says he has been hot and listless since lunchtime and has refused his tea. On examination there are several pinpoint and blotchy purple lesions on his thighs that remain visible when the skin is pressed. What should the GP do?

options.A: Take blood for a full blood count and decide once the result is back
options.B: Give parenteral benzylpenicillin and arrange emergency hospital transfer
options.C: Prescribe oral antibiotics and review tomorrow
options.D: Advise antipyretics and give safety-netting advice
options.E: Refer to the next paediatric outpatient clinic

correct_answer: B. Give parenteral benzylpenicillin and arrange emergency hospital transfer
why_correct: A febrile, listless child with a non-blanching rash must be managed as suspected meningococcal disease. In primary care NICE advises giving intramuscular or intravenous benzylpenicillin as soon as possible, provided this does not delay transfer, and arranging an emergency ambulance to hospital.
why_wrong: A. Waiting for blood results delays life-saving treatment. C. Oral antibiotics and next-day review are inadequate for invasive bacterial infection. D. Treating the fever alone ignores a life-threatening cause. E. An outpatient referral is far too slow.
pearl: If benzylpenicillin is unavailable or contraindicated in the community, transfer to hospital must still not be delayed.
thinking: Child with fever and lethargy ↓ Rash that does not blanch ↓ Suspected meningococcal disease ↓ Benzylpenicillin if it does not delay transfer ↓ Emergency ambulance to hospital
exam_trap: A, Taking blood and deciding once the result is back — it feels thorough, but a normal blood count does not exclude meningococcal disease and the delay is dangerous.
takeaway: In the community, give benzylpenicillin and transfer urgently for a feverish child with a non-blanching rash.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN4402). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 41-year-old man is given intravenous midazolam for sedation during an endoscopy. Shortly afterwards he cannot be roused and his breathing becomes slow and shallow despite airway support. He takes no regular medicines and has never had a seizure. Which drug specifically reverses this effect?
why_correct: Midazolam is a benzodiazepine, and flumazenil is a competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine binding site of the GABA-A receptor. Reversing over-sedation from procedural benzodiazepines in a patient with no seizure history or benzodiazepine dependence is the situation in which flumazenil is most appropriate.
why_wrong: A. Naloxone reverses opioids, not benzodiazepines. B. Atropine treats bradycardia and cholinergic excess. D. Protamine reverses heparin. E. Glucagon is used for beta-blocker toxicity and hypoglycaemia.
pearl: Flumazenil has a shorter duration of action than many benzodiazepines, so re-sedation can occur and patients need continued monitoring.
thinking: Intravenous midazolam given ↓ Unrousable with respiratory depression ↓ Benzodiazepine over-sedation ↓ No seizure history or dependence ↓ Flumazenil
exam_trap: A, Naloxone — opioids are often co-administered for endoscopy, but naloxone has no effect on benzodiazepine-induced sedation.
takeaway: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and is safest in procedural over-sedation without seizure risk.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN8541). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 72-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on ramipril and spironolactone is admitted to the medical ward feeling weak. His blood results show severe hyperkalaemia, and a 12-lead ECG shows peaked T waves. The registrar asks you which drug should be given first to protect his heart from arrhythmia while other measures are arranged. Which treatment is most appropriate?
why_correct: Intravenous calcium (gluconate or chloride) stabilises the myocardial cell membrane within minutes and is given first when hyperkalaemia is accompanied by ECG changes. It does not lower the serum potassium, so it must be followed by treatments that shift potassium into cells and remove it from the body. His ramipril and spironolactone should also be stopped.
why_wrong: A. Insulin with glucose shifts potassium into cells but does not protect the myocardium directly; it follows calcium. B. Salbutamol is an adjunct to shift potassium and does not stabilise the membrane. D. Potassium binders remove potassium slowly over hours and do nothing for the immediate arrhythmia risk. E. Furosemide may increase renal potassium loss but is slow and does not protect the heart.
pearl: The effect of intravenous calcium lasts only about 30 to 60 minutes, so the ECG should be repeated and further doses given if changes persist.
thinking: Severe hyperkalaemia ↓ ECG changes present ↓ Immediate risk is arrhythmia ↓ Stabilise the myocardium first ↓ Intravenous calcium, then shift and remove potassium
exam_trap: A, Intravenous insulin with glucose — it is essential and lowers potassium quickly, but it does not protect the heart and should follow calcium.
takeaway: Hyperkalaemia with ECG changes: give intravenous calcium first to stabilise the heart.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN8550). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 47-year-old man is transferred from a minor injuries unit after telling the nurse practitioner that he swallowed most of a large tub of paracetamol at around 9 o'clock that morning. It is now early afternoon. He has no abdominal pain, his observations are normal and he is otherwise healthy. Which blood test is most useful in estimating his risk of liver damage?

options.C: Paracetamol concentration measured at a known interval after the ingestion

correct_answer: C. Paracetamol concentration measured at a known interval after the ingestion
why_correct: His ingestion was a single episode at a known time more than 4 hours ago, so the plasma paracetamol concentration can be plotted on the treatment nomogram. A level on or above the treatment line indicates the need for acetylcysteine, while liver tests, INR and renal function provide a baseline.
why_wrong: A. Troponin assesses myocardial injury, which is not a feature of paracetamol overdose. B. Salicylate concentration assesses aspirin poisoning. D. Ferritin and iron are relevant to iron poisoning or iron status. E. Amylase does not assess hepatotoxicity.
pearl: Liver tests are often normal in the first hours after a toxic paracetamol dose, so they cannot be used on their own to decide against treatment.
thinking: Single ingestion at a known time ↓ More than 4 hours ago ↓ Asymptomatic with normal observations ↓ Quantify the risk ↓ Plot the timed paracetamol level on the nomogram
exam_trap: B, Salicylate concentration — it is part of many overdose screens, but it measures aspirin exposure and says nothing about paracetamol liver risk.
takeaway: Measure paracetamol at a known time after a single ingestion to estimate hepatotoxicity risk.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN4639). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Pulse oximetry in carbon monoxide poisoning
stem: A 50-year-old man is rescued from a smoke-filled house fire and brought to the emergency department. He is drowsy, has a pounding headache and is vomiting. A finger probe shows oxygen saturation of 99% on room air, and the nurse suggests oxygen is not needed. Why is this reading unreliable?

options.A: Finger probes measure blood pressure rather than oxygen content
options.B: The probe cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so it overestimates true saturation
options.C: Carbon monoxide converts haemoglobin to methaemoglobin
options.D: Carbon monoxide markedly reduces arterial oxygen tension
options.E: Pulse oximetry readings are independent of haemoglobin

correct_answer: B. The probe cannot tell carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin, so it overestimates true saturation
why_correct: Standard two-wavelength pulse oximeters cannot distinguish carboxyhaemoglobin from oxyhaemoglobin because they absorb light similarly, so the displayed saturation is falsely normal. Arterial oxygen tension is also usually normal, which adds to false reassurance. He needs high-flow oxygen immediately and carboxyhaemoglobin measured by co-oximetry.
why_wrong: A. Pulse oximeters estimate haemoglobin oxygen saturation, not blood pressure. C. Carbon monoxide forms carboxyhaemoglobin rather than methaemoglobin. D. Dissolved oxygen tension is typically preserved despite tissue hypoxia. E. Pulse oximetry relies entirely on light absorption by haemoglobin.
pearl: Give 100% oxygen via a non-rebreather mask to anyone with suspected carbon monoxide poisoning, regardless of the saturation reading.
thinking: Smoke inhalation with headache, vomiting and drowsiness ↓ Saturation reads near normal ↓ Oximeter reads carboxyhaemoglobin as oxygenated ↓ True oxygen content is reduced ↓ Treat with high-flow oxygen and check co-oximetry
exam_trap: D, Carbon monoxide markedly reduces arterial oxygen tension — it sounds logical, but the arterial tension usually stays normal, which is why the numbers mislead.
takeaway: A normal pulse oximeter reading does not exclude carbon monoxide poisoning.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN4785). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 48-year-old man takes the first tablet of co-amoxiclav prescribed by his GP while still in the pharmacy. Within fifteen minutes he develops an itchy blotchy rash spreading across his body, becomes short of breath and has an audible wheeze. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Anaphylaxis is a severe, rapidly developing systemic hypersensitivity reaction with airway, breathing or circulation problems, usually with skin changes. Sudden widespread rash plus breathlessness and wheeze within minutes of a penicillin-based antibiotic fits this. Treatment is intramuscular adrenaline without delay and an emergency ambulance.
why_wrong: A. Viral exanthems develop over days with fever and are not linked to wheeze within minutes of a drug. B. Cellulitis is localised infection of the skin, not a generalised rash with bronchospasm. C. Psoriasis causes chronic scaly plaques. E. Tinea corporis is a slowly enlarging fungal ring lesion.
pearl: Skin features are absent in a minority of anaphylaxis cases, so airway, breathing or circulation problems after a trigger should prompt adrenaline even without a rash.
thinking: Penicillin-type antibiotic just taken ↓ Rapid widespread itchy rash ↓ Breathlessness and wheeze ↓ Skin plus breathing involvement ↓ Anaphylaxis
exam_trap: A, Viral exanthem — a widespread rash suggests a viral cause, but the sudden onset with wheeze minutes after a drug indicates anaphylaxis.
takeaway: A sudden rash with wheeze after a drug is anaphylaxis until proven otherwise.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN5116). Do not return to the live bank.
