stem: Paramedics attend a 38-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes who has collapsed at her office desk. She groans but does not follow commands and has a weak gag reflex. Her fingerprick glucose is very low. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.A: Rub glucose gel onto her gums
options.E: Give intravenous glucose or intramuscular glucagon

correct_answer: E. Give intravenous glucose or intramuscular glucagon
why_correct: In a hypoglycaemic patient who cannot safely swallow, glucose must be delivered by a parenteral route. Intravenous glucose works quickly if access can be obtained, and intramuscular glucagon is the alternative if it cannot. Once alert, she needs oral long-acting carbohydrate and review of the cause.
why_wrong: A. Gel on the gums risks aspiration in someone with impaired swallowing and absorbs unreliably. B. Insulin would worsen hypoglycaemia. C. Hydrocortisone treats adrenal crisis, not insulin-induced hypoglycaemia. D. Tablets cannot be swallowed safely with reduced consciousness.
pearl: In adults, 10% glucose is preferred to 50% for intravenous treatment because it is less irritant to veins and causes less extravasation injury.
thinking: Type 1 diabetes with collapse ↓ Very low capillary glucose ↓ Reduced consciousness and weak gag ↓ Nothing by mouth ↓ Intravenous glucose or intramuscular glucagon
exam_trap: A, Rub glucose gel onto her gums — it feels safer than drinking, but with a weak gag it can still be aspirated and absorption is unreliable.
takeaway: Unconscious hypoglycaemia needs intravenous glucose or intramuscular glucagon.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN10321). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: Ten days after a caesarean birth, a 34-year-old woman collapses in the emergency department waiting area. She is tachycardic and grey, her systolic blood pressure is 70 mmHg, her neck veins are distended and she is hypoxic. A bedside echocardiogram shows a dilated right ventricle. What is the immediate priority?

options.A: Calculate the Wells score and refer her to the ambulatory PE clinic
options.B: Request a D-dimer and wait for the result before treating
options.C: Start oral apixaban and arrange outpatient CT pulmonary angiography
options.D: Resuscitate and treat as suspected high-risk pulmonary embolism, with immediate senior involvement and consideration of thrombolysis
options.E: Admit to a ward bed for CT pulmonary angiography within 24 hours, with LMWH

correct_answer: D. Resuscitate and treat as suspected high-risk pulmonary embolism, with immediate senior involvement and consideration of thrombolysis
why_correct: She has obstructive shock with right ventricular dilatation in a high-risk postpartum period, which is suspected high-risk PE. The immediate priority is resuscitation and treatment for massive PE, involving senior emergency, medical and obstetric teams and considering systemic thrombolysis, because delay is associated with death.
why_wrong: A. Scoring tools and ambulatory pathways are for haemodynamically stable patients. B. Waiting for a D-dimer delays life-saving treatment and the result would not change management. C. Outpatient pathways are inappropriate in shock. E. Planning imaging over 24 hours ignores her instability.
pearl: Bedside echocardiography showing right ventricular dilatation can justify thrombolysis in a patient with suspected PE who is too unstable to go to CT.
thinking: Postpartum woman ↓ Collapse with hypotension and raised neck veins ↓ Hypoxia and dilated right ventricle ↓ Obstructive shock from suspected PE ↓ Resuscitate and treat as high-risk PE immediately
exam_trap: A, Wells score — structured scoring is how PE work-up usually begins, but it applies to stable patients and wastes time in shock.
takeaway: In suspected PE with shock, resuscitate and treat as high-risk PE immediately rather than following the stable-patient pathway.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN207). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: On a medical ward, a 40-year-old man with known epilepsy has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure that stops after 2 minutes. Afterwards he stays unresponsive, but he is breathing regularly and normally and has a good central pulse. There is no concern about a neck injury. Which position should he be placed in?

options.A: Sitting upright in the bedside chair
options.B: Flat on his back with a pillow under his head
options.C: Face down with the head turned, checked at the next observation round
options.D: Supine with chest compressions started while a defibrillator is brought
options.E: The recovery position, with his airway maintained and breathing watched continuously

correct_answer: E. The recovery position, with his airway maintained and breathing watched continuously
why_correct: After the seizure he is unresponsive but breathing normally with a pulse, so he is not in cardiac arrest. The recovery position keeps the tongue from obstructing the airway and lets saliva or vomit drain, and he needs continuous observation until he recovers.
why_wrong: A. An unconscious patient cannot hold his head up and may obstruct his airway or fall. B. Lying flat on the back risks airway obstruction and aspiration. C. Prone positioning restricts breathing and he must not be left between observation rounds. D. Compressions are not indicated when there is normal breathing and a pulse.
pearl: A seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without recovery in between, is status epilepticus and needs emergency benzodiazepine treatment.
thinking: Seizure has stopped ↓ Unresponsive in post-ictal phase ↓ Normal breathing and pulse present ↓ Airway at risk from tongue and secretions ↓ Recovery position with continuous monitoring
exam_trap: B, Lying flat on his back — it seems comfortable and easy to observe, but in an unconscious patient the tongue can fall back and vomit can be aspirated.
takeaway: An unconscious patient who is breathing normally should be placed in the recovery position and watched continuously.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN9093). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Natriuretic peptide in suspected heart failure
stem: During a telephone consultation, a 61-year-old woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes says that over several months she has had to stop for breath when walking her dog, and her rings feel tight. Her GP is worried about cardiac failure. Which investigation best helps decide how likely this diagnosis is?
why_correct: NICE NG106 recommends an NT-proBNP level for people with suspected chronic heart failure. The result indicates how likely heart failure is and how quickly echocardiography and specialist assessment are needed; a normal level makes the diagnosis unlikely. Her hypertension and diabetes are risk factors that make the test appropriate here.
why_wrong: A. Ferritin assesses iron stores, which matter once heart failure is diagnosed, but it cannot estimate the probability of the condition. B. HbA1c monitors her diabetes and says nothing about cardiac function. C. D-dimer is used to rule out venous thromboembolism and does not assess heart failure. E. Spirometry assesses airflow obstruction and is useful for lung causes of breathlessness, not for gauging heart failure.
pearl: Very high NT-proBNP levels mean the patient should be seen by a specialist and have echocardiography within two weeks, whereas moderately raised levels allow up to six weeks.
thinking: Gradual exertional breathlessness and fluid retention ↓ Risk factors: hypertension and diabetes ↓ Suspected chronic heart failure ↓ Need a test of likelihood ↓ Measure NT-proBNP
exam_trap: E, Spirometry — it is a reasonable test for breathlessness generally, but it investigates the lungs and does not tell the GP how likely heart failure is.
takeaway: NT-proBNP is the test that estimates the likelihood of heart failure and guides the urgency of referral.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN1136). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: At a heart failure clinic review, an 80-year-old man says that within minutes of reclining fully he becomes short of breath, so he now sleeps sitting well up against a backrest; if he slips down in the night, he needs to haul himself up again before his breathing eases. What is the medical term for this?
why_correct: His breathlessness comes on soon after lying flat and is relieved by sitting up, which is orthopnoea. It occurs because recumbency increases venous return to a failing left ventricle, raising pulmonary capillary pressure.
why_wrong: A. Platypnoea is the reverse: breathlessness that worsens on sitting or standing upright and eases on lying down. B. Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea refers to being woken from sleep by breathlessness some hours after lying down, rather than breathlessness within minutes of reclining. D. Haemoptysis means coughing up blood. E. Claudication is exertional leg pain from arterial disease.
pearl: Platypnoea, often with orthodeoxia, suggests an intracardiac or intrapulmonary right-to-left shunt, such as a patent foramen ovale or hepatopulmonary syndrome.
thinking: Known heart failure ↓ Breathless within minutes of reclining ↓ Relieved by sitting up ↓ Posture-dependent left heart congestion ↓ Orthopnoea
exam_trap: B, Paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea — it is also a night-time heart failure symptom, but it describes being woken from sleep hours later, not breathlessness as soon as he lies back.
takeaway: Orthopnoea is breathlessness within minutes of lying flat, relieved by sitting up.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN5126). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 76-year-old man with known left ventricular systolic dysfunction is visited at home by the community heart failure nurse. Over the past week his breathing has worsened, he has started sleeping propped up, and both ankles have swollen further; his home scales show a steady rise in weight. Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Bilateral cellulitis of the lower legs

why_correct: Progressive breathlessness, new orthopnoea, increasing ankle oedema and steady weight gain in a man with known left ventricular dysfunction indicate fluid congestion from decompensated heart failure. He needs prompt review of his diuretic and a search for a trigger, with hospital admission if he is unstable.
why_wrong: A. Cellulitis is usually unilateral with red, hot, tender skin and does not cause orthopnoea or weight gain. C. Pneumonia causes fever, cough and focal signs, not orthopnoea with bilateral oedema. D. Asthma causes variable wheeze and is not associated with peripheral oedema or weight gain. E. Bilateral DVT is rare and would not explain orthopnoea or worsening breathlessness of this pattern.
pearl: Rising daily weight is often the earliest sign of decompensation, appearing before symptoms worsen.
thinking: Known left ventricular dysfunction ↓ Worsening breathlessness and new orthopnoea ↓ Increasing bilateral ankle oedema ↓ Steady weight gain ↓ Acute decompensated heart failure
exam_trap: E, Bilateral deep vein thrombosis — swollen legs suggest clots, but bilateral DVT is uncommon and does not explain orthopnoea and weight gain.
takeaway: Worsening breathlessness, orthopnoea, oedema and weight gain in known heart failure signal decompensation.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN536). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A woman phones NHS 111 about her 86-year-old father, who has a weak heart. She says that for a fortnight he has refused to go to bed and spends each night in his armchair, explaining that reclining fully makes him puffed out and that he only feels comfortable sitting up. Which symptom is he describing?
why_correct: Breathlessness when lying flat that is relieved by sitting up is orthopnoea. Recumbency redistributes blood from the legs and abdomen into the chest, increasing pulmonary venous pressure in a failing left ventricle; this is why many people with heart failure end up sleeping in a chair.
why_wrong: A. Trepopnoea is breathlessness when lying on one side but not the other, not when lying flat. C. Vertigo is a false sense of movement or spinning. D. Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness. E. Claudication is cramping leg pain on walking due to arterial insufficiency.
pearl: A new need to sleep in a chair in someone with heart failure suggests worsening congestion and should prompt a review of fluid status and diuretic dose.
thinking: Known heart failure ↓ Avoids lying flat ↓ Breathless when reclined, comfortable upright ↓ Posture-related pulmonary congestion ↓ Orthopnoea
exam_trap: A, Trepopnoea — it is also a positional breathlessness, but it depends on which side the patient lies, not on lying flat versus sitting up.
takeaway: Sleeping in a chair to avoid breathlessness on lying flat is orthopnoea, a classic sign of heart failure.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN5126). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: Paramedics are called to a 71-year-old man at home with an hour of central chest heaviness spreading to his jaw, with vomiting and clamminess. Their 12-lead recording shows convex ST elevation in II, III and aVF, with reciprocal ST depression in aVL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
why_correct: Typical ischaemic pain with autonomic features and regional convex ST elevation in the inferior leads, plus reciprocal depression, is diagnostic of an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction. NICE NG185 recommends immediate referral for primary PCI if it can be delivered within 120 minutes of when fibrinolysis could have been given. Paramedics should pre-alert the heart attack centre and take him directly there.
why_wrong: B. Pericarditis gives widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal change. C. Anterior STEMI involves V1 to V4. D. Lateral STEMI involves I, aVL, V5 and V6, whereas aVL is depressed here. E. Posterior STEMI shows ST depression and tall R waves in V1 to V3.
pearl: Reciprocal ST depression supports a STEMI and argues strongly against pericarditis.
thinking: Ischaemic pain with vomiting and sweating ↓ Regional convex ST elevation in II, III, aVF ↓ Reciprocal depression in aVL ↓ Inferior STEMI ↓ Direct transfer for primary PCI
exam_trap: B, Acute pericarditis — ST elevation in several leads tempts this, but pericarditis is diffuse, concave and lacks reciprocal depression.
takeaway: Regional ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal change is an inferior STEMI needing immediate reperfusion.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN352). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Exertional syncope in structural heart disease
stem: A 64-year-old woman with known moderate aortic stenosis is seen in cardiology clinic after losing consciousness without warning while cycling up a hill. She came round quickly. Which feature of her history most strongly points to a cardiac cause?
why_correct: In aortic stenosis the fixed outflow obstruction prevents cardiac output rising during exercise, so blood pressure falls and cerebral perfusion fails. Syncope during exertion, especially without prodrome, is therefore a red flag for a cardiac cause. NICE CG109 recommends urgent specialist assessment, and symptomatic aortic stenosis is an indication to consider valve replacement.
why_wrong: A. Hay fever and antihistamines do not cause exertional collapse. C. Hunger alone does not explain sudden collapse during effort. D. Travel sickness is not linked to cardiac syncope. E. Back pain is irrelevant to the cause of collapse.
pearl: Angina, syncope and breathlessness are the classic symptoms of aortic stenosis, and any of them marks the point at which prognosis worsens without intervention.
thinking: Known aortic stenosis ↓ Collapse while cycling uphill ↓ No warning ↓ Fixed outflow cannot meet demand ↓ Exertional syncope = cardiac red flag
exam_trap: C, Feeling hungry after skipping lunch — it hints at hypoglycaemia, but that causes gradual symptoms and would not explain sudden collapse on exertion.
takeaway: Exertional syncope in structural heart disease needs urgent cardiac assessment.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN1312). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Exertional syncope as a red flag
stem: A 64-year-old woman sees her GP about a blackout last week. She was walking briskly uphill to catch a bus when she lost consciousness without any warning, and she was back to normal within a minute. Afterwards she felt a little sweaty. Years ago she fainted once at a hot, crowded wedding. Which feature of her story most strongly suggests a cardiac cause?

options.A: Fainting once at a crowded wedding
options.D: No tongue biting or limb jerking

why_correct: Syncope that occurs during exertion is a red flag for structural heart disease, such as aortic stenosis or cardiomyopathy, or for arrhythmia. NICE advises an ECG and specialist cardiovascular assessment within 24 hours for anyone with exertional syncope. The absence of a prodrome adds to concern.
why_wrong: A. A single faint in a hot crowded setting is typical of a vasovagal episode. C. Sweating after an episode is common in reflex syncope and does not point to the heart. D. The absence of seizure features helps exclude epilepsy but does not identify a cardiac cause. E. Rapid recovery is typical of any syncope, cardiac or reflex.
pearl: Other red flags for cardiac syncope include an abnormal ECG, heart failure, new breathlessness, a heart murmur, and a family history of sudden cardiac death under 40.
thinking: Transient loss of consciousness with full recovery ↓ Occurred during exertion ↓ No warning symptoms ↓ Exertional syncope is a cardiac red flag ↓ Needs ECG and urgent cardiovascular assessment
exam_trap: A, Fainting at a crowded wedding — a past faint can seem relevant, but that history supports benign vasovagal syncope and draws attention away from the exertional trigger.
takeaway: Syncope during exertion should be treated as cardiac until proven otherwise.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN6844). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: During a school swimming gala a 14-year-old boy goes limp in the water and is pulled out by the lifeguard; he comes round quickly on the poolside. His uncle died suddenly in his twenties with no cause found. In hospital, his echocardiogram shows a structurally normal heart. Which inherited condition should be considered?
why_correct: Congenital long QT syndrome is an inherited channelopathy that predisposes to torsades de pointes and sudden death. Syncope during exercise, particularly swimming, is characteristic of the type 1 form, and a family history of unexplained sudden death in a young relative is a major clue. A normal echocardiogram fits an electrical rather than structural disorder.
why_wrong: A. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes exertional syncope but would show thickened myocardium on echocardiogram. B. Marfan syndrome threatens the aorta and valves rather than causing arrhythmic collapse with a normal heart. D. Rheumatic heart disease is acquired and causes valve damage visible on echocardiogram. E. Familial hypercholesterolaemia causes premature coronary disease, not syncope in a teenager with a normal heart.
pearl: Drugs that prolong the QT interval, such as macrolides, some antipsychotics and ondansetron, should be avoided in long QT syndrome, and beta-blockers are first-line treatment.
thinking: Teenager collapses while swimming ↓ Young relative died suddenly without explanation ↓ Structurally normal heart on echocardiogram ↓ Suggests an inherited electrical disorder ↓ Long QT syndrome
exam_trap: A, Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy — exertional syncope with family sudden death is classic for it, but the normal echocardiogram points away from a structural cause.
takeaway: Exertional syncope, especially while swimming, with a structurally normal heart and family sudden death suggests long QT syndrome.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN1914). Do not return to the live bank.

stem:
While waiting for a routine hernia repair, a 45-year-old builder has a pre-operative ECG. The nurse calls you because the printout shows bizarre, chaotic complexes in several leads. On reaching the bedside you find him sitting up chatting, warm and well perfused, with a regular radial pulse at a normal rate. He has had no palpitations or dizziness.

What is the most appropriate first step?

options.A: Put him in the resuscitation bay and give intravenous amiodarone
options.B: Start treatment for an acute coronary syndrome and send a troponin
options.C: Look for sources of interference and repeat the trace with electrodes correctly placed
options.D: Apply defibrillator pads and arrange synchronised DC cardioversion
options.E: Put out a cardiac arrest call for presumed ventricular tachycardia

correct_answer: C. Look for sources of interference and repeat the trace with electrodes correctly placed
why_correct: A well, talking patient with a normal palpable pulse cannot be in a haemodynamically significant arrhythmia, so the trace is most likely artefact from movement, tremor, shivering or poor electrode contact. The right step is to check the leads and skin contact and repeat the ECG before any treatment. Always treat the patient rather than the paper.
why_wrong: A. Amiodarone has serious adverse effects and should not be given on the basis of an unverified trace in a well patient. B. Nothing in his history or examination suggests acute coronary syndrome. D. Cardioversion is not indicated in an asymptomatic patient with a normal pulse. E. A man who is talking with a palpable pulse is not in cardiac arrest.
pearl: Common causes of ECG artefact include patient movement, shivering, Parkinsonian tremor, loose or dried electrodes and limb lead reversal.
thinking: Alarming-looking trace ↓ Patient well, talking, normal pulse ↓ Clinical picture does not match the ECG ↓ Suspect artefact ↓ Check electrodes and repeat before acting
exam_trap: E, Calling the arrest team — the chaotic complexes look like a malignant rhythm, but a conscious patient with a normal pulse is not in cardiac arrest and the trace needs verifying first.
takeaway: When an ECG looks dangerous but the patient is well with a normal pulse, exclude artefact and repeat the trace before treating.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN712). Do not return to the live bank.

stem:
Patrick, 74, has his annual diabetes review with the practice nurse, who notices that his pulse is irregular. An ECG later confirms atrial fibrillation. The GP talks to him about starting edoxaban and explains what it is mainly intended to prevent.

Which complication is the anticoagulant chiefly given to reduce?
why_correct: Atrial fibrillation allows thrombus to form in the left atrium, which can embolise to the brain and cause ischaemic stroke. With age and diabetes his stroke risk is raised, and anticoagulation substantially reduces cardioembolic stroke. This is the main reason for offering it.
why_wrong: A. Reflux is not a complication of AF and is not prevented by anticoagulation. B. AF does not cause pneumothorax. D. Macular degeneration is unrelated to AF. E. Gout is unrelated to AF and is not prevented by anticoagulants.
pearl: AF-related strokes tend to be larger and more disabling than other ischaemic strokes because the emboli often occlude large cerebral arteries.
thinking: Irregular pulse found at review ↓ ECG confirms AF ↓ Atrial stasis forms thrombus ↓ Embolism to the brain ↓ Anticoagulation prevents ischaemic stroke
exam_trap: A, Gastro-oesophageal reflux — gastrointestinal problems come to mind because anticoagulants can cause GI bleeding, but that is a risk of treatment rather than the complication it prevents.
takeaway: Anticoagulation in AF is given to prevent embolic ischaemic stroke.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN7093). Do not return to the live bank.

stem:
A 69-year-old woman attends a cardiology follow-up clinic. She has had persistent atrial fibrillation for a year and her heart rate is well controlled on bisoprolol. She has no chest pain, breathlessness or dizziness.

Which serious complication does this rhythm most predispose her to?
why_correct: Even when the rate is controlled and she feels well, AF causes atrial blood stasis and thrombus formation. Emboli most commonly travel to the cerebral circulation, making ischaemic stroke the major serious complication of AF. Rate control relieves symptoms but does not remove this risk.
why_wrong: A. Pancreatitis is not caused by AF. B. Duodenal ulceration is not a complication of AF. C. Osteoarthritis is unrelated to cardiac rhythm. E. Lens opacity (cataract) is not caused by AF.
pearl: AF also increases the risk of heart failure and is associated with vascular dementia, but stroke is its most feared complication.
thinking: Persistent AF, rate controlled ↓ Atria still not contracting effectively ↓ Stasis and thrombus formation persist ↓ Systemic embolism ↓ Ischaemic stroke
exam_trap: B, Duodenal ulceration — gastrointestinal bleeding is a concern in people on anticoagulants, but ulceration is not a complication of the arrhythmia itself.
takeaway: Good rate control does not remove the stroke risk of atrial fibrillation.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN7093). Do not return to the live bank.

presentation: Clinical probability scoring in suspected DVT
stem:
An 80-year-old man in a nursing home has been less mobile since a stroke two months ago. The visiting advanced nurse practitioner finds his left calf swollen and tender along the deep veins, and nothing else seems a better explanation. She needs to decide how probable a DVT is before referring him for tests.

Which assessment tool is appropriate?
why_correct: The two-level DVT Wells score is the tool NICE NG158 recommends for estimating the clinical probability of DVT. His immobility, localised deep vein tenderness and calf swelling all add points, and the result determines whether he needs proximal leg vein ultrasound or a D-dimer first.
why_wrong: B. The Abbreviated Mental Test screens cognitive function. C. CURB-65 grades severity of community-acquired pneumonia. D. CHA2DS2-VA estimates stroke risk in atrial fibrillation. E. The Glasgow Coma Scale measures level of consciousness.
pearl: Paralysis, paresis or recent plaster immobilisation of the leg is one of the DVT Wells criteria.
thinking: Immobile after stroke ↓ Swollen calf with deep vein tenderness ↓ Suspected DVT ↓ Estimate probability with Wells score ↓ Choose ultrasound or D-dimer
exam_trap: D, CHA2DS2-VA — he has had a stroke and thrombotic risk is on the mind, but this score predicts stroke in atrial fibrillation, not the probability of a DVT.
takeaway: The Wells score is the clinical probability tool for suspected DVT.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN799). Do not return to the live bank.

stem:
A 52-year-old office worker sees her GP with two days of discomfort behind her right knee. Examination shows a small, soft, slightly tender swelling in the popliteal fossa, suggesting a Baker's cyst. The calf is not swollen. Because a clot cannot be excluded, the GP scores her and finds DVT is unlikely.

Which test is generally used next?
why_correct: When the two-level DVT Wells score shows DVT is unlikely, NICE NG158 recommends a D-dimer test as the next step. A negative D-dimer makes DVT very unlikely, while a positive result means proximal leg vein ultrasound is needed. An alternative diagnosis such as a Baker's cyst lowers the Wells score but does not remove the need to exclude a clot.
why_wrong: A. Troponin measures myocardial injury. C. Spirometry tests lung function. D. CT head has no role in suspected DVT. E. Echocardiography does not detect leg vein thrombosis.
pearl: A ruptured Baker's cyst can closely mimic DVT with sudden calf pain and swelling, and the two can coexist.
thinking: Posterior knee pain with possible Baker's cyst ↓ DVT still possible ↓ Two-level Wells: DVT unlikely ↓ D-dimer next ↓ Ultrasound only if D-dimer is positive
exam_trap: E, Echocardiography — it is a familiar cardiovascular investigation, but it images the heart and gives no information about thrombus in the leg veins.
takeaway: For suspected DVT with a low Wells score, the next test is a D-dimer.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN801). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: Over six weeks, a 63-year-old librarian has had raised readings at three practice nurse appointments, the latest being 164/98 mmHg. She has no symptoms, fundoscopy is normal and urine dipstick shows no protein or blood. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.D: Continue monthly clinic readings for a year
options.E: Offer ambulatory blood pressure monitoring to confirm the diagnosis

correct_answer: E. Offer ambulatory blood pressure monitoring to confirm the diagnosis
why_correct: Her readings are persistently raised but not severe, and there are no symptoms or signs of acute end-organ injury. NICE recommends confirming the diagnosis with ambulatory monitoring before labelling and treating hypertension. This is a routine outpatient pathway, not an emergency.
why_wrong: A. Intravenous antihypertensives are only for hypertensive emergencies with acute organ damage. B. A hypertensive emergency requires acute target-organ damage, which is absent here. C. Same-day assessment is for severe readings with red-flag features. D. Repeated clinic readings delay diagnosis and do not exclude a white-coat effect.
pearl: Ambulatory monitoring should capture at least two readings an hour during waking hours, using an average of at least 14 daytime readings.
thinking: Persistently raised clinic readings ↓ Not in the severe range ↓ No symptoms or signs of organ damage ↓ Not an emergency ↓ Confirm with ABPM
exam_trap: C, Arrange same-day medical assessment — repeatedly raised readings feel worrying, but without severe values or red flags the correct step is outpatient confirmation.
takeaway: Persistent non-severe clinic hypertension should be confirmed with ambulatory monitoring rather than treated as an emergency.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN1129). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is advised by NHS 111 to attend the emergency department after a blackout. The registrar takes a careful history to judge whether the episode is likely to have a cardiac cause. Which feature of her history would most strongly suggest that it does?

options.A: Similar faints since her teens, previously diagnosed as vasovagal
options.B: Feeling sick and clammy just before losing consciousness
options.C: Fainting while having a blood test
options.D: Collapsing while running for a bus
options.E: Fainting after standing for a long time at a crowded concert

correct_answer: D. Collapsing while running for a bus
why_correct: Loss of consciousness during exertion is a red flag for structural or electrical heart disease, such as aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or an arrhythmia. NICE recommends urgent cardiovascular assessment, within 24 hours, for exertional syncope. The other features point towards benign reflex syncope.
why_wrong: A. A long history of typical vasovagal faints is reassuring. B. A prodrome of nausea and sweating is typical of reflex syncope. C. Fainting during venepuncture is a classic vasovagal trigger. E. Prolonged standing in a hot, crowded place is a typical trigger for reflex syncope.
pearl: Other red flags for cardiac syncope include new or unexplained breathlessness, a heart murmur, an abnormal ECG, a family history of sudden death under 40 and syncope while lying down.
thinking: Transient loss of consciousness ↓ Look for triggers and prodrome ↓ Typical triggers suggest reflex syncope ↓ Exertion is a cardiac red flag ↓ Urgent cardiovascular assessment
exam_trap: A, Similar faints since her teens — a long history of blackouts may seem worrying, but recurrent typical vasovagal episodes are reassuring rather than suggestive of heart disease.
takeaway: Syncope during exertion should be treated as cardiac until proven otherwise.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN6844). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 79-year-old woman living in a care home is found to have an irregularly irregular pulse, and an ECG confirms atrial fibrillation. Bisoprolol has now settled her heart rate. Her daughter phones the GP to ask why apixaban is also being recommended. What is the main purpose of this treatment?

options.A: To convert her heart back to sinus rhythm
options.B: To slow her heart rate further
options.D: To reduce her risk of an embolic stroke

correct_answer: D. To reduce her risk of an embolic stroke
why_correct: In atrial fibrillation, the atria do not contract effectively, so blood stagnates, particularly in the left atrial appendage, and clots can form and travel to the brain. Anticoagulation substantially reduces this risk of embolic stroke. The decision is based on stroke risk assessment balanced against bleeding risk, and rate control alone does not remove the clot risk.
why_wrong: A. Apixaban has no effect on rhythm; cardioversion or antiarrhythmic drugs are used for that. B. Rate control is achieved by her beta-blocker, not anticoagulation. C. Anticoagulants do not lower blood pressure. E. Apixaban has no effect on cholesterol; statins are used for that.
pearl: Aspirin is not recommended by NICE for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation; a direct oral anticoagulant is usually first choice.
thinking: Atrial fibrillation confirmed ↓ Rate now controlled ↓ Stagnant atrial blood forms clots ↓ Clots embolise to the brain ↓ Anticoagulate to prevent stroke
exam_trap: B, To slow her heart rate further — rate control is the most visible part of AF management, but anticoagulants do not affect heart rate; their role is stroke prevention.
takeaway: Anticoagulation in atrial fibrillation is given to prevent embolic stroke, not to control rate or rhythm.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN7093). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 92-year-old woman admitted to a medical ward because she was struggling to mobilise at home becomes disorientated and agitated on her third day. The ward team draws up a list of possible triggers to check. Which of the following is a common precipitant of delirium that should be on that list?

options.C: Infection, such as a urinary or chest infection

correct_answer: C. Infection, such as a urinary or chest infection
why_correct: Infection is one of the commonest precipitants of delirium in older people, particularly urinary and respiratory infections, including those acquired in hospital. The other options are stable chronic conditions that would not explain an acute change. Observations, examination and targeted tests help identify an infection.
why_wrong: A. Presbyopia is a stable age-related change in near vision and does not precipitate delirium. B. Stable osteoarthritis does not cause acute confusion, although uncontrolled pain could. D. Chronic psoriasis is not a recognised precipitant. E. Well-controlled thyroid disease does not cause an acute change.
pearl: Hospital-acquired infection, dehydration, new medicines, pain and urinary catheters are all frequent triggers of delirium that begins after admission.
thinking: Very elderly inpatient ↓ New confusion on day three ↓ Delirium likely ↓ List reversible triggers ↓ Infection is among the commonest
exam_trap: B, Stable osteoarthritis — pain can trigger delirium, so it may tempt, but stable, controlled arthritis does not cause an acute change.
takeaway: Infection is a leading precipitant of delirium in older inpatients.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN10474). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: At an annual review, the practice nurse sees an 87-year-old man whose daughter says he has become thinner and weaker over the past year. He now takes much longer to walk to the corner shop, needs help with bathing and has given up gardening. There is no single disease to explain the change. Which concept best describes this presentation?
why_correct: Frailty is a clinical syndrome of reduced reserve and resilience, often shown by unintentional weight loss, weakness, slow walking speed, low activity and growing dependence. It is not explained by a single disease. Identifying it allows targeted support, medicine review and planning of care.
why_wrong: A. Stable angina causes exertional chest pain rather than general decline. B. Migraine causes recurrent headaches. C. Hyperthyroidism can cause weight loss but there is no single disease here and no thyroid features. E. Appendicitis is an acute surgical illness.
pearl: Simple tools such as gait speed, the timed up and go test or the PRISMA-7 questionnaire can help identify frailty (NICE NG56).
thinking: Unintentional weight loss ↓ Weakness and slow walking ↓ Reduced activity ↓ Growing dependence with no single disease ↓ Frailty
exam_trap: C, Hyperthyroidism — weight loss can suggest it, but slowness, low activity and dependence without other thyroid features describe frailty.
takeaway: Weight loss, weakness, slowness and growing dependence together describe frailty.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN1716). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: Paramedics attend a 79-year-old man who has fallen at home for the second time this month. He is uninjured and declines to go to hospital, so they pass his details to his GP, who sees him the next day. His observations are normal and he is keen to stay independent. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Arrange a hip X-ray and reassure him if no fracture is seen
options.B: Stop all his regular medicines immediately
options.C: Carry out a multifactorial falls risk assessment
options.D: Prescribe antibiotics in case an infection caused the falls
options.E: Advise bed rest at home until his mobility improves

correct_answer: C. Carry out a multifactorial falls risk assessment
why_correct: Two falls in a short period identify him as at high risk of further falls. A multifactorial falls risk assessment looks at medicines, gait and balance, cardiovascular causes, vision, cognition, footwear and home hazards, and leads to targeted interventions that help him stay independent. Paramedic referral after a non-conveyed fall is a common route into this assessment.
why_wrong: A. He has no injury or hip pain, and a normal X-ray would not address why he is falling. B. Medicines should be reviewed selectively; stopping everything abruptly is unsafe. D. Antibiotics are inappropriate without evidence of infection. E. Bed rest leads to deconditioning and makes falls more likely.
pearl: Many ambulance services refer older people who have fallen but are not taken to hospital to community falls services for assessment.
thinking: Second fall this month ↓ Uninjured, not taken to hospital ↓ Wishes to stay independent ↓ High risk of further falls ↓ Multifactorial falls risk assessment
exam_trap: A, Hip X-ray and reassurance — imaging feels thorough after a fall, but he has no injury and reassurance would leave the causes of his falls unaddressed.
takeaway: An older person with recurrent falls needs a multifactorial assessment, not just exclusion of fracture.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN10509). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: At a flu vaccination appointment, an 85-year-old man mentions to the practice nurse that he has fallen three times this year. He was not hurt, but his wife has started to worry when he goes out alone. Which response is most appropriate?

options.A: Reassure him that falling is a normal part of getting older
options.B: Suggest he uses a wheelchair whenever he leaves the house
options.C: Offer a multifactorial falls risk assessment to find modifiable causes
options.D: Arrange a DXA scan and take no further action
options.E: Provide a pendant alarm instead of any further assessment

correct_answer: C. Offer a multifactorial falls risk assessment to find modifiable causes
why_correct: Older people who report recurrent falls should be offered a multifactorial falls risk assessment. This looks at causes such as medicines, gait and balance, vision, postural hypotension, continence, cognition, footwear and home hazards, so that targeted interventions can be offered to prevent further falls.
why_wrong: A. Falls are common in later life but are not inevitable, and many causes can be modified. B. A wheelchair would reduce activity and worsen strength and balance. D. Bone health matters, but a DXA scan alone does nothing to reduce falls. E. An alarm helps summon help after a fall but does not prevent one.
pearl: Strength and balance training is one of the most effective single interventions for preventing falls in older people living at home.
thinking: Three falls this year ↓ Recurrent falls mean increased future risk ↓ Many causes are modifiable ↓ Multifactorial assessment identifies them ↓ Offer targeted interventions
exam_trap: E, A pendant alarm — it is a sensible addition and reassures relatives, but it only shortens time on the floor after a fall and leaves the causes unaddressed.
takeaway: Recurrent falls warrant a multifactorial assessment for modifiable risk factors.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN10509). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 46-year-old man breaks his wrist after tripping on a kerb, and a DXA scan arranged by the fracture liaison service shows osteoporosis. He has never needed to shave daily, has little chest hair and fathered no children despite trying. On examination he is tall with long legs, has mild gynaecomastia and small, firm testes. Testosterone is low and FSH and LH are high. Which diagnosis is most likely?
why_correct: Lifelong poor virilisation, infertility, tall stature, gynaecomastia and small firm testes with raised gonadotrophins indicate primary hypogonadism present since puberty. This is the typical adult presentation of undiagnosed Klinefelter syndrome. Long-standing testosterone deficiency explains his osteoporosis and low-trauma fracture, and testosterone replacement should be considered.
why_wrong: A. Cushing's syndrome causes osteoporosis but with central obesity, striae and proximal myopathy rather than lifelong hypogonadism. B. Hyperprolactinaemia causes secondary hypogonadism with low or normal gonadotrophins. C. Kallmann syndrome causes hypogonadism with low gonadotrophins and anosmia. D. Haemochromatosis usually causes secondary hypogonadism from pituitary iron deposition, with acquired rather than lifelong features.
pearl: Many men with Klinefelter syndrome are not diagnosed until adulthood, through infertility, osteoporosis or hypogonadism.
thinking: Low-trauma fracture with osteoporosis in a man ↓ Lifelong poor virilisation and infertility ↓ Tall with gynaecomastia ↓ Small firm testes, high LH and FSH ↓ Klinefelter syndrome
exam_trap: C, Kallmann syndrome — it also causes lifelong hypogonadism, but gonadotrophins are low and the testes are not firm.
takeaway: Klinefelter syndrome can present late in adult men with osteoporosis and primary hypogonadism.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN6056). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 5-year-old boy is assessed by the community paediatrician for delayed speech, poor eye contact and hand-flapping. He has a long face, prominent ears and very flexible finger joints. His mother developed early menopause at 36, and her brother has a learning disability. DNA testing confirms a CGG repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene. Which inheritance pattern best describes this condition?

options.B: X-linked, with expansion of the repeat through the generations

correct_answer: B. X-linked, with expansion of the repeat through the generations
why_correct: Fragile X syndrome is caused by a CGG trinucleotide repeat expansion in the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. A premutation carried by a woman tends to expand into a full mutation when passed to her children, so severity increases in later generations, which is anticipation. The mother's early menopause suggests she carries a premutation, which causes fragile X-associated primary ovarian insufficiency.
why_wrong: A. The FMR1 gene is on the X chromosome and the disease depends on repeat expansion. C. Mitochondrial conditions affect all children of an affected mother and are not caused by FMR1 repeat expansion. D. Fragile X is not autosomal, and many carriers are unaffected or mildly affected. E. Y-linked disorders pass from father to son only, and here the condition comes through the mother's family.
pearl: Fragile X premutation carriers can develop premature ovarian insufficiency in women and a late-onset tremor-ataxia syndrome, mainly in men.
thinking: Boy with learning disability and autistic features ↓ Long face, large ears, lax joints ↓ Affected maternal uncle, mother with early menopause ↓ FMR1 CGG repeat expansion ↓ X-linked with anticipation
exam_trap: D, Autosomal dominant — affected people in two generations suggest dominance, but the gene is on the X chromosome and expansion occurs through female transmission.
takeaway: Fragile X syndrome is X-linked and shows anticipation through maternal CGG repeat expansion.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN3868). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 48-year-old woman saw a private gastroenterologist, who recommended a branded version of omeprazole for her reflux. At her GP practice she is told the NHS prescription will be issued generically, and she asks whether the generic will work as well. What is the key principle to explain?

options.A: Branded medicines are safer than generic versions
options.B: The generic contains the same active ingredient as the branded product
options.C: Generic medicines usually work less well than brands
options.D: Generic prescribing needs specialist approval on the NHS
options.E: The generic is a similar but chemically different compound

correct_answer: B. The generic contains the same active ingredient as the branded product
why_correct: A generic medicine contains the same active ingredient as the branded version and is required to be bioequivalent, so it produces the same therapeutic effect. Prescribing by generic name is standard NHS practice and helps reduce cost without reducing effectiveness. She can expect the same benefit from generic omeprazole.
why_wrong: A. Branding does not make a medicine safer; both must meet the same standards. C. Generics are not inherently less effective, as bioequivalence must be shown. D. Generic prescribing is routine and needs no specialist approval. E. The active ingredient is identical, not a different compound.
pearl: Generic prescribing is encouraged across the NHS; brand prescribing is reserved for situations where formulations are not interchangeable.
thinking: Patient worried generic is inferior ↓ Generic contains the same active ingredient ↓ Must be bioequivalent ↓ Same expected therapeutic effect ↓ Generic prescribing is routine NHS practice
exam_trap: A, Branded medicines are safer — many patients assume a brand means higher quality, but generics must meet the same regulatory standards for quality and safety.
takeaway: A generic medicine has the same active ingredient as the brand and is expected to work the same way.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ11606). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: At a community pharmacy, a 63-year-old woman asks to buy naproxen for a flare of lower back pain. On questioning she says she was treated for a bleeding duodenal ulcer two years ago. The pharmacist advises against it and suggests she speaks to her GP. What is the main reason for this advice?
correct_answer: C. Recurrent ulceration with gastrointestinal bleeding
why_correct: NSAIDs block cyclo-oxygenase and reduce the prostaglandins that protect the stomach and duodenal lining. A previous ulcer, especially one that bled, is one of the strongest risk factors for NSAID-related ulceration and bleeding. NICE CKS advises avoiding NSAIDs in people with a history of peptic ulcer, or using gastroprotection and specialist advice if one cannot be avoided.
why_wrong: A. Gum overgrowth is linked to phenytoin, ciclosporin and calcium channel blockers, not NSAIDs. B. NSAIDs do not usually cause hypoglycaemia. D. Hearing loss is a feature of aminoglycosides and loop diuretics, not standard NSAID doses. E. NSAIDs do not affect thyroid function.
pearl: The highest risk of NSAID-related gastrointestinal bleeding is in people over 65, people with previous ulcer or bleeding, and people also taking anticoagulants, antiplatelets, SSRIs or corticosteroids.
thinking: Request for an over-the-counter NSAID ↓ Past bleeding duodenal ulcer ↓ NSAIDs reduce protective mucosal prostaglandins ↓ High risk of recurrent ulcer and bleeding ↓ Advise avoidance and a GP review
exam_trap: D, Sensorineural hearing loss — ototoxicity is a known drug adverse effect so it sounds credible, but it belongs to aminoglycosides and high-dose loop diuretics, not naproxen.
takeaway: A previous peptic ulcer, especially one that bled, is a strong reason to avoid NSAIDs because of the risk of further ulceration and bleeding.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAQ12213). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 73-year-old woman is admitted to a surgical ward from the emergency department with small bowel obstruction. She is under a cardiologist, a rheumatologist and her GP, and her daughter has brought a carrier bag full of medicine boxes. The surgical doctor must write up her drug chart. Which step is most important for her safety?

options.A: Copy the GP summary record as the final admission list
options.B: Prescribe from what she remembers and confirm with the GP after discharge
options.C: Check her medicines against at least two reliable sources and resolve any differences
options.D: Continue the list from her last hospital discharge letter unchanged
options.E: Hold all regular medicines until a pharmacist can see her next week

correct_answer: C. Check her medicines against at least two reliable sources and resolve any differences
why_correct: NICE NG5 recommends medicines reconciliation on admission, comparing at least two reliable sources such as the GP record, the patient's own medicines, specialist letters and the patient or carer. Any discrepancies, such as specialist-only drugs missing from the GP list, are resolved and documented. This prevents omissions, duplications and dosing errors, ideally within 24 hours of admission.
why_wrong: A. A GP summary can miss specialist or recently changed medicines. B. Memory alone is unreliable and delays correction. D. An old discharge letter may be out of date. E. Withholding all regular medicines risks harm from missed doses of important drugs.
pearl: Reconciliation should also include over-the-counter, herbal and specialist-supplied medicines, which often do not appear on the GP record.
thinking: Admission with several prescribers ↓ Risk of omissions and duplication ↓ Collect at least two reliable sources ↓ Compare and resolve differences ↓ Document an accurate list
exam_trap: A, Copying the GP summary record — it looks like the most official source, but it often lacks hospital specialist drugs and recent changes.
takeaway: On admission, reconcile medicines using at least two reliable sources and resolve every discrepancy.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN10495). Do not return to the live bank.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and heart failure telephones NHS 111. Since yesterday she has had repeated vomiting from a stomach bug going round her family and can keep down only sips of water. She takes metformin and dapagliflozin. She asks whether she should keep taking her diabetes tablets. What is the most appropriate advice about her dapagliflozin?

options.A: Keep taking it as normal to avoid a rise in blood glucose
options.B: Take double the usual dose because illness increases glucose
options.C: Stop it temporarily and restart once she is eating and drinking normally
options.D: Continue it and add gliclazide while she is unwell
options.E: Replace it with modified-release metformin until she recovers

correct_answer: C. Stop it temporarily and restart once she is eating and drinking normally
why_correct: SGLT2 inhibitors such as dapagliflozin increase the risk of diabetic ketoacidosis during dehydrating illness, and this can occur with only modestly raised glucose, so it is easily missed. Sick-day guidance is therefore to pause the drug while vomiting or unable to eat and drink, and restart 24 to 48 hours after she is eating and drinking normally. She should also be told to seek urgent help if she develops abdominal pain, breathlessness or drowsiness.
why_wrong: A. Continuing it during dehydration increases the risk of ketoacidosis. B. Increasing the dose would worsen volume depletion and ketoacidosis risk. D. Adding a sulfonylurea when she cannot eat risks hypoglycaemia and leaves the SGLT2 inhibitor risk unchanged. E. Metformin should also usually be paused during dehydrating illness, so substituting it is inappropriate.
pearl: Euglycaemic diabetic ketoacidosis is a recognised hazard of SGLT2 inhibitors, so ketones should be checked in unwell patients even when glucose is not very high.
thinking: Vomiting and unable to eat or drink ↓ Takes an SGLT2 inhibitor ↓ Risk of ketoacidosis with near-normal glucose ↓ Sick-day rule applies ↓ Pause it and restart when eating and drinking
exam_trap: A, Keep taking it to prevent high glucose — fear of hyperglycaemia is intuitive, but the main danger with this drug in dehydrating illness is ketoacidosis.
takeaway: Pause SGLT2 inhibitors during dehydrating illness because of the risk of ketoacidosis.
review_note: Rejected by the clinical reviewer, 17 Oct 2026 (duplicate of PAN10068). Do not return to the live bank.
